papers.research_question: This paper investigates why safety alignment in large language models is vulnerable to jailbreak attacks due to the concentration of safety mechanisms in a few attention heads, and whether distributing these mechanisms across more heads can enhance robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RDSHA to identify safety-critical attention heads and proposes AHD, a training strategy that distributes safety capabilities across more heads, enhancing robustness against jailbreak attacks while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: This work addresses concentrated safety vulnerabilities in LLMs by introducing RDSHA for identifying critical heads and proposing AHD to distribute safety, which improves resistance to jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are concentrated in a small subset of attention heads, as identified by RDSHA.
Ablating these critical attention heads significantly compromises model safety, increasing harmfulness rates.
Jailbreak attacks exploit this sparsity by selectively bypassing or suppressing safety-critical heads.
AHD distributes safety alignment across more attention heads, making models more robust to ablation and jailbreak attacks.
Models trained with AHD maintain overall utility without increasing over-refusal of benign queries.
papers.limitation: Reliance on a limited subset of the Alpaca dataset as a utility anchor during fine-tuning, preventing conclusive determination of utility drops.
future_direction: Access more diverse and comprehensive utility datasets for fine-tuning.
Explore alternative utility-preserving objectives and multi-task learning strategies.
papers.abstract: Current safety alignment for large language models(LLMs) continues to present vulnerabilities, given that adversarial prompting can effectively bypass their safety measures.Our investigation shows that these safety mechanisms predominantly depend on a limited subset of attention heads: removing or ablating these heads can severely compromise model safety. To identify and evaluate these safety-critical components, we introduce RDSHA, a targeted ablation method that leverages the model's refusal direction to pinpoint attention heads mostly responsible for safety behaviors. Further analysis shows that existing jailbreak attacks exploit this concentration by selectively bypassing or manipulating these critical attention heads. To address this issue, we propose AHD, a novel training strategy designed to promote the distributed encoding of safety-related behaviors across numerous attention heads. Experimental results demonstrate that AHD successfully distributes safety-related capabilities across more attention heads. Moreover, evaluations under several mainstream jailbreak attacks show that models trained with AHD exhibit considerably stronger safety robustness, while maintaining overall functional utility.

papers.title: Surgery: Mitigating Harmful Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Attention Sink
papers.research_question: Can we design a fine-tuning-stage defense that leverages the model’s intrinsic mechanisms to proactively prevent the model from learning harmful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a fine-tuning-stage defense called Surgery that uses sink divergence suppression to steer attention heads away from learning harmful patterns, thereby mitigating harmful fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Surgery is an effective fine-tuning-stage defense that leverages attention sink mechanisms to mitigate harmful fine-tuning and maintain model safety.
papers.key_findings:
Sink divergence separates attention heads into two distinct groups (positive and negative).
The number of attention heads with positive sink divergence increases with the model's harmfulness during harmful fine-tuning.
Disabling attention heads with positive sink divergence suppresses the model's harmful behavior.
The proposed Surgery method significantly reduces harmful scores while maintaining fine-tuning accuracy across various settings.
Surgery outperforms existing fine-tuning-stage defenses on multiple benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Suppression in the early layers was relatively limited.
The evaluation covered only small-scale models.
future_direction: Enhance the model’s defensive capabilities by improving suppression in early layers.
Evaluate the method on larger or proprietary models.
papers.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can invalidate safety alignment of large language models, exposing significant safety risks. In this paper, we utilize the attention sink mechanism to mitigate harmful fine-tuning. Specifically, we first measure a statistic named \emph{sink divergence} for each attention head and observe that \emph{different attention heads exhibit two different signs of sink divergence}. To understand its safety implications, we conduct experiments and find that the number of attention heads of positive sink divergence increases along with the increase of the model's harmfulness when undergoing harmful fine-tuning. Based on this finding, we propose a separable sink divergence hypothesis -- \emph{attention heads associating with learning harmful patterns during fine-tuning are separable by their sign of sink divergence}. Based on the hypothesis, we propose a fine-tuning-stage defense, dubbed Surgery. Surgery utilizes a regularizer for sink divergence suppression, which steers attention heads toward the negative sink divergence group, thereby reducing the model's tendency to learn and amplify harmful patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Surgery improves defense performance by 5.90\%, 11.25\%, and 9.55\% on the BeaverTails, HarmBench, and SorryBench benchmarks, respectively. Source code is available on https://github.com/Lslland/Surgery.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Language Models are Homer Simpson! Safety Re-Alignment of Fine-tuned Language Models through Task Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How can the safety of fine-tuned language models, which is often compromised during fine-tuning, be restored?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RESTA, a simple method that adds a safety vector to the weights of a fine-tuned model to restore its safety alignment with minimal performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: RESTA effectively restores safety to fine-tuned language models by adding a safety vector, significantly reducing harmfulness with minimal performance loss, and generalizes across tasks and languages.
papers.key_findings:
RESTA significantly reduces the unsafety score of fine-tuned models across multiple domains (Chinese, Hindi, English, Code, Math) and languages.
RESTA is effective for both Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) and Full Fine-Tuning (Full-FT).
Using DARE (Drop and REscale) on delta parameters can further enhance the effectiveness of RESTA, especially in PEFT.
The safety vector generalizes to out-of-domain safety benchmarks and across languages (Chinese, Vietnamese).
The performance degradation due to adding the safety vector is minimal (average reduction of 2.41% in PEFT and 0.47% in Full-FT across tasks).
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to Llama-2-7B due to budget constraints, not larger models like Llama-2-70B.
Lack of extensive hyperparameter tuning for γ and p.
No analysis of safety vector transferability across language models.
future_direction: Analysis of safety vector transferability across language models.
Further investigation of DARE on full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Analyzing the Noise Robustness of Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Why are adversarial examples (slightly perturbed images) misclassified by deep neural networks, and how do the datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a visual analysis tool, AEVis, which extracts and visualizes datapaths (critical neurons and connections) of adversarial and normal examples to explain the root cause of misclassifications.
papers.conclusion: AEVis effectively helps experts analyze the prediction process of adversarial examples and identify the root cause of misclassifications through multi-level datapath visualization and interaction.
papers.key_findings:
The datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge at specific layers, revealing where and how the model's predictions change.
The root cause of misclassification can be traced to specific neurons or feature maps that fail to detect key features or are activated by adversarial noise.
A constrained datapath extraction method reduces randomness and better preserves diverging and merging patterns for comparison.
Multi-level visualization (network, layer, neuron) combined with contribution analysis enables systematic investigation of adversarial misclassifications.
Case studies on ResNet101 and a 6-layer CNN demonstrate the method's ability to identify failure modes such as missed object parts or spurious feature detection.
papers.limitation:
Time complexity of datapath extraction and contribution analysis (several minutes offline, ~5 seconds for contribution analysis).
Visual scalability for very deep CNNs (thousands of layers) and when comparing many datapaths.
Generalization to other DNN types (RNNs, AEs, DGMs) and data types (text, video) requires extension of datapath extraction and visualization methods.
future_direction: Develop targeted defense solutions based on discovered root causes of misclassification.
Enable online detection and monitoring of adversarial examples with streaming visualizations.
Generalize AEVis to analyze other types of DNNs (RNNs, autoencoders, generative models) and data types (text, video).
papers.abstract: Adversarial examples, generated by adding small but intentionally imperceptible perturbations to normal examples, can mislead deep neural networks (DNNs) to make incorrect predictions. Although much work has been done on both adversarial attack and defense, a fine-grained understanding of adversarial examples is still lacking. To address this issue, we present a visual analysis method to explain why adversarial examples are misclassified. The key is to compare and analyze the datapaths of both the adversarial and normal examples. A datapath is a group of critical neurons along with their connections. We formulate the datapath extraction as a subset selection problem and solve it by constructing and training a neural network. A multi-level visualization consisting of a network-level visualization of data flows, a layer-level visualization of feature maps, and a neuron-level visualization of learned features, has been designed to help investigate how datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge in the prediction process. A quantitative evaluation and a case study were conducted to demonstrate the promise of our method to explain the misclassification of adversarial examples.

papers.title: The Hidden Space of Safety: Understanding Preference-Tuned LLMs in Multilingual context
papers.research_question: How does alignment (preference tuning) affect the hidden representations of LLMs across different languages, and does it generalize effectively beyond English?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that alignment induces a separation between safe and unsafe representations in the hidden space for English, but this effect is significantly weaker for other languages, highlighting a monolingual bias in current preference-tuning methods.
papers.conclusion: State-of-the-art preference-tuned models exhibit a monolingual bias, with alignment being effective in English but inconsistent across other languages, underscoring the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure robust multilingual safety.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment improves cluster separation between harmful and harmless prompts in English but shows inconsistent and weaker effects in Hindi, Chinese, and German.
Quantitative metrics (Bhattacharyya Distance, Silhouette Score) confirm stronger alignment-induced separation in English compared to other languages.
In a parallel text-detoxification setting, alignment fails to induce a clear distribution shift for Hindi, indicating language-dependent representation learning.
The study finds that some models (e.g., for Hindi) can show greater cluster separation in the unaligned reference model than in the aligned model, indicating potential alignment degradation.
Current alignment strategies, optimized on English-centric preference data, do not generalize robustly to multilingual settings, leading to safety inconsistencies.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily focuses on safety alignment, overlooking other critical domains such as multi-modality, reasoning, instruction-following, or planning due to the lack of standardized multilingual benchmarks for these tasks.
Only three non-English languages (Hindi, Chinese, German), all medium-resource, are evaluated, limiting generalizability to low-resource languages.
The dataset consists of 5,000 sentences, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world multilingual scenarios.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to low-resource languages to better understand alignment disparities.
Use a broader dataset to further validate findings across different linguistic and cultural contexts.
Prioritize multilingual preference collection and explore synthetic techniques to transfer alignment knowledge from English to other languages.
papers.abstract: Alignment tuning has enabled large language models to excel in reasoning, instruction-following, and minimizing harmful generations. However, despite their widespread deployment, these models exhibit a monolingual bias, raising concerns about the effectiveness of alignment across languages. Current alignment methods predominantly focus on English, leaving it unclear how alignment mechanism generalize to multilingual settings. To address this, we conduct a systematic analysis of distributional shifts in the embedding space of LLMs before and after alignment, uncovering its impact on model behavior across diverse languages. We leverage the alignment-induced separation in safety space as a quantitative tool to measure how alignment enforces safety constraints. Our study evaluates seven LLMs using balanced toxicity datasets and parallel text-detoxification benchmarks, revealing substantial disparities in the latent representation space between high-resource and low-resource languages. These findings underscore the need for language-specific fine-tuning to ensure fair, reliable and robust multilingual alignment. Our insights provide a foundation for developing truly safe multilingual LLMs, emphasizing the urgency of addressing alignment gaps in underrepresented languages.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to build inherently interpretable large language models (LLMs) for text classification and text generation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models (CB-LLMs), a framework to build inherently interpretable LLMs for text classification and generation that matches black-box model performance while providing transparency and control.
papers.conclusion: CB-LLMs provide a framework for building interpretable LLMs without sacrificing performance, enabling transparent reasoning, controlled generation, and enhanced safety and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
CB-LLMs for text classification achieve accuracy competitive with or superior to black-box models and provide faithful explanations as measured by human evaluation.
CB-LLMs for text generation match black-box performance and enable controllable generation, including toxicity reduction through neuron steering.
The method scales to large datasets (e.g., 560k samples) and automates concept labeling without expensive LLM API calls.
Human evaluations show CB-LLMs provide better explanations than prior interpretable models (TBM & C3M).
Concept unlearning in CB-LLMs can improve prediction fairness by removing biased or subjective concepts.
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models (CB-LLMs), a novel framework for building inherently interpretable Large Language Models (LLMs). In contrast to traditional black-box LLMs that rely on limited post-hoc interpretations, CB-LLMs integrate intrinsic interpretability directly into the LLMs -- allowing accurate explanations with scalability and transparency. We build CB-LLMs for two essential NLP tasks: text classification and text generation. In text classification, CB-LLMs is competitive with, and at times outperforms, traditional black-box models while providing explicit and interpretable reasoning. For the more challenging task of text generation, interpretable neurons in CB-LLMs enable precise concept detection, controlled generation, and safer outputs. The embedded interpretability empowers users to transparently identify harmful content, steer model behavior, and unlearn undesired concepts -- significantly enhancing the safety, reliability, and trustworthiness of LLMs, which are critical capabilities notably absent in existing models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/CB-LLMs.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Safety Arithmetic: A Framework for Test-time Safety Alignment of Language Models by Steering Parameters and Activations
papers.research_question: Can an existing approach handle all three scenarios (base models, supervised fine-tuned models, and edited models) efficiently for safety alignment while preserving model general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFETY ARITHMETIC, a training-free framework for test-time safety alignment of language models across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited models by removing harmful directions from parameters and steering activations toward safe responses.
papers.conclusion: SAFETY ARITHMETIC effectively improves safety measures, mitigates over-safety, and preserves utility across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited language models, outperforming existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAFETY ARITHMETIC significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple safety datasets (e.g., AdvBench, DangerousQA) for base, fine-tuned, and edited models.
The framework maintains model utility on standard benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) and reduces over-safety (lower refusal rates on benign queries).
The Harm Direction Removal (HDR) stage using top-k parameter selection and the Safety Alignment (Safe-Align) stage using an in-context safety vector (ICV) are both effective components.
The method outperforms baselines like HDR with TIES, HDR with Task Vector, and Safe-Align with ICV alone.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models with up to 7 billion parameters, not representing larger models (>7B).
In HDR, selecting the top k parameters in the harm vector is crucial; changing too many parameters may impair the model's general abilities.
In Safe-Align, determining the fraction of the ICV vector to add to token representations during inference is important.
future_direction: Optimize hyperparameters, such as the scaling factor for harm vector application and the strength of in-context vectors, to enhance the framework's precision, robustness, and reliability across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Ensuring the safe alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human values is critical as they become integral to applications like translation and question answering. Current alignment methods struggle with dynamic user intentions and complex objectives, making models vulnerable to generating harmful content. We propose Safety Arithmetic, a training-free framework enhancing LLM safety across different scenarios: Base models, Supervised fine-tuned models (SFT), and Edited models. Safety Arithmetic involves Harm Direction Removal to avoid harmful content and Safety Alignment to promote safe responses. Additionally, we present NoIntentEdit, a dataset highlighting edit instances that could compromise model safety if used unintentionally. Our experiments show that Safety Arithmetic significantly improves safety measures, reduces over-safety, and maintains model utility, outperforming existing methods in ensuring safe content generation.

papers.title: A Guardrail for Safety Preservation: When Safety-Sensitive Subspace Meets Harmful-Resistant Null-Space
papers.research_question: How to preserve safety alignment of large language models during fine-tuning on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GuardSpace, a framework that initializes low-rank adapters in a safety-irrelevant subspace and constrains their updates to a harmful-resistant null space, preserving safety alignment during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: GuardSpace effectively preserves safety alignment during fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art trade-off between safety and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
GuardSpace achieves lower harmful score and higher fine-tuning accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods like AsFT.
GuardSpace maintains low harmful score across different model architectures (Llama-2, Qwen-2, Gemma-2).
GuardSpace is robust to varying proportions of unsafe examples in the fine-tuning data.
The safety-sensitive subspace initialization and harmful-resistant null space projector are both effective components.
The method requires only a few hundred harmful prompts to construct an effective null space projector.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in diverse tasks, yet their safety alignment remains fragile during adaptation. Even when fine-tuning on benign data or with low-rank adaptation, pre-trained safety behaviors are easily degraded, leading to harmful responses in the fine-tuned models. To address this challenge, we propose GuardSpace, a guardrail framework for preserving safety alignment throughout fine-tuning, composed of two key components: a safety-sensitive subspace and a harmful-resistant null space. First, we explicitly decompose pre-trained weights into safety-relevant and safety-irrelevant components using covariance-preconditioned singular value decomposition, and initialize low-rank adapters from the safety-irrelevant ones, while freezing safety-relevant components to preserve their associated safety mechanism. Second, we construct a null space projector that restricts adapter updates from altering safe outputs on harmful prompts, thereby maintaining the original refusal behavior. Experiments with various pre-trained models on multiple downstream tasks demonstrate that GuardSpace achieves superior performance over existing methods. Notably, for Llama-2-7B-Chat fine-tuned on GSM8K, GuardSpace outperforms the state-of-the-art method AsFT, reducing the average harmful score from 14.4% to 3.6%, while improving the accuracy from from 26.0% to 28.0%.

papers.title: Light Alignment Improves LLM Safety via Model Self-Reflection with a Single Neuron
papers.research_question: How can we design a lightweight safety alignment method that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance model intrinsic capabilities and external guidance, thereby improving safety without compromising utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight safety alignment method (NGSD) that uses a single neuron as a gating mechanism to balance intrinsic model capabilities with external safety guidance, achieving a favorable safety-utility trade-off with minimal training overhead.
papers.conclusion: Lightweight and targeted safety alignment mechanisms, such as NGSD, can provide meaningful safety improvements without significantly degrading utility, offering a practical direction for deploying safer large language models.
papers.key_findings:
NGSD reduces attack success rates across multiple jailbreak attack scenarios (e.g., GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN).
NGSD preserves utility on benign tasks (e.g., GSM8K, Just-Eval) better than strong baselines like SafeDecoding.
The neuron-based gating mechanism is more robust and responsive than alternative gating methods (EMA, SMG).
The method demonstrates strong generalization and transferability across model scales and families.
NGSD requires only training a small expert model and efficiently transfers to larger models within the same family.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness in more open-ended or long-horizon settings remains unclear.
Differences in tokenization limit generalization across model families.
future_direction: Explore adaptive risk estimation and more general safety alignment strategies.
Conduct cross-family evaluation under diverse generation regimes.
papers.abstract: The safety of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly emerged as a fundamental aspect of their development. Existing safety alignment for LLMs is predominantly achieved through post-training methods, which are computationally expensive and often fail to generalize well across different models. A small number of lightweight alignment approaches either rely heavily on prior-computed safety injections or depend excessively on the model's own capabilities, resulting in limited generalization and degraded efficiency and usability during generation. In this work, we propose a safety-aware decoding method that requires only low-cost training of an expert model and employs a single neuron as a gating mechanism. By effectively balancing the model's intrinsic capabilities with external guidance, our approach simultaneously preserves utility and enhances output safety. It demonstrates clear advantages in training overhead and generalization across model scales, offering a new perspective on lightweight alignment for the safe and practical deployment of large language models. Code: https://github.com/Beijing-AISI/NGSD.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: GateBreaker: Gate-Guided Attacks on Mixture-of-Expert LLMs
papers.research_question: How can the safety alignment of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models be compromised via a training-free, lightweight attack framework that identifies and disables safety-critical neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GateBreaker, a training-free attack framework that compromises safety alignment in MoE LLMs by identifying and disabling a small subset of safety-critical neurons, significantly increasing attack success rates with minimal utility degradation.
papers.conclusion: MoE LLMs exhibit concentrated safety mechanisms that can be efficiently compromised via neuron-level interventions, highlighting the need for more robust and distributed safety alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
MoE safety mechanisms are concentrated within a small subset of neurons coordinated by sparse routing.
Selectively disabling approximately 3% of neurons in targeted expert layers increases the average attack success rate from 7.4% to 64.9% across eight aligned MoE LLMs.
Safety neurons transfer across models within the same family, enabling effective one-shot transfer attacks.
GateBreaker generalizes to MoE Vision Language Models, increasing ASR from 20.8% to 60.9% on unsafe image inputs.
GateBreaker substantially outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method SAFEx, achieving more than double the average ASR.
papers.limitation:
The attack requires white-box access to the model's internal states (gate logits and neuron activations).
The effectiveness of safety neuron identification depends on the quality and coverage of the malicious and benign prompt datasets used for profiling.
future_direction: Developing defenses such as adversarial training and monitoring gate activation patterns.
Exploring robust routing mechanisms that are less vulnerable to targeted neuron suppression.
Extending the analysis to other emerging MoE architectures and alignment methods.
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have advanced the scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) by activating only a sparse subset of parameters per input, enabling state-of-the-art performance with reduced computational cost. As these models are increasingly deployed in critical domains, understanding and strengthening their alignment mechanisms is essential to prevent harmful outputs. However, existing LLM safety research has focused almost exclusively on dense architectures, leaving the unique safety properties of MoEs largely unexamined. The modular, sparsely-activated design of MoEs suggests that safety mechanisms may operate differently than in dense models, raising questions about their robustness. In this paper, we present GateBreaker, the first training-free, lightweight, and architecture-agnostic attack framework that compromises the safety alignment of modern MoE LLMs at inference time. GateBreaker operates in three stages: (i) gate-level profiling, which identifies safety experts disproportionately routed on harmful inputs, (ii) expert-level localization, which localizes the safety structure within safety experts, and (iii) targeted safety removal, which disables the identified safety structure to compromise the safety alignment. Our study shows that MoE safety concentrates within a small subset of neurons coordinated by sparse routing. Selective disabling of these neurons, approximately 3% of neurons in the targeted expert layers, significantly increases the averaged attack success rate (ASR) from 7.4% to 64.9% against the eight latest aligned MoE LLMs with limited utility degradation. These safety neurons transfer across models within the same family, raising ASR from 17.9% to 67.7% with one-shot transfer attack. Furthermore, GateBreaker generalizes to five MoE vision language models (VLMs) with 60.9% ASR on unsafe image inputs.

papers.title: NeuroStrike: Neuron-Level Attacks on Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How can the sparse, specialized safety neurons introduced by alignment techniques in LLMs be exploited to create effective and generalizable attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroStrike, a neuron-level attack framework that exploits sparse, specialized safety neurons to compromise safety alignment in LLMs, achieving high attack success rates in both white-box (via pruning) and black-box (via profiling) settings.
papers.conclusion: Safety alignment in LLMs is fragile and relies on sparse, attackable safety neurons, posing a significant threat that requires new defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (less than 0.6% of neurons in a layer), specialized, and transferable across model variants and families.
Pruning these neurons in white-box models increases the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 12.1% to 76.9% across 11 open-source LLMs.
The attack generalizes to multimodal LLMs, achieving 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs after pruning.
Safety neuron transferability enables effective black-box attacks, raising the average ASR from 3.5% to 63.7% across five proprietary models, including Google's Gemini family.
The utility of pruned models on standard NLU benchmarks remains largely intact, indicating targeted degradation of safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The white-box attack requires access to model weights and neuron activations.
The black-box attack assumes the availability of a suitable open-weight surrogate model for profiling.
Pruning safety neurons can lead to moderate utility degradation on some reasoning-heavy tasks.
future_direction: Developing defenses against neuron-level attacks.
Improving the robustness of safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is critical for the ethical deployment of large language models (LLMs), guiding them to avoid generating harmful or unethical content. Current alignment techniques, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, remain fragile and can be bypassed by carefully crafted adversarial prompts. Unfortunately, such attacks rely on trial and error, lack generalizability across models, and are constrained by scalability and reliability. This paper presents NeuroStrike, a novel and generalizable attack framework that exploits a fundamental vulnerability introduced by alignment techniques: the reliance on sparse, specialized safety neurons responsible for detecting and suppressing harmful inputs. We apply NeuroStrike to both white-box and black-box settings: In the white-box setting, NeuroStrike identifies safety neurons through feedforward activation analysis and prunes them during inference to disable safety mechanisms. In the black-box setting, we propose the first LLM profiling attack, which leverages safety neuron transferability by training adversarial prompt generators on open-weight surrogate models and then deploying them against black-box and proprietary targets. We evaluate NeuroStrike on over 20 open-weight LLMs from major LLM developers. By removing less than 0.6% of neurons in targeted layers, NeuroStrike achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 76.9% using only vanilla malicious prompts. Moreover, Neurostrike generalizes to four multimodal LLMs with 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs. Safety neurons transfer effectively across architectures, raising ASR to 78.5% on 11 fine-tuned models and 77.7% on five distilled models. The black-box LLM profiling attack achieves an average ASR of 63.7% across five black-box models, including the Google Gemini family.

papers.title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
papers.research_question: Can aligned behavior be transferred even when the teacher and student differ in architecture, task, and training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BIRD, a framework for transferring aligned behavior by distilling the structure of a teacher's internal representations into a student, without requiring shared data or tasks, and shows that transfer success is predictable by teacher representation properties.
papers.conclusion: BIRD provides a flexible, data-free mechanism for transferring aligned behavior across models and domains, advancing weak-to-strong generalization and enabling scalable, reusable alignment.
papers.key_findings:
BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods in transferring out-of-distribution robustness, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the strongest baseline.
BIRD remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is 25× smaller than the student.
Three interpretable properties of the teacher’s representation space (task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success.
BIRD can improve weak-to-strong generalization in NLP when combined with soft-label distillation, though the effect is not universal.
Transfer success is predictable and actionable, offering practical guidance for teacher and layer selection.
papers.limitation:
Core analyses focus on robustness in vision, with only preliminary results in NLP.
Transfer success is likely bounded by the student’s capacity and task complexity.
Currently supervise alignment at a single layer; multi-layer or hierarchical extensions may be needed.
Effectiveness depends on the teacher; if the teacher encodes misaligned behaviors, BIRD may transfer them.
future_direction: Extending BIRD to other behaviors (e.g., honesty) and modalities (e.g., multimodal reasoning).
Quantifying the saturation effect of transfer success more precisely.
Exploring multi-layer or hierarchical extensions to capture deeper structural alignment.
papers.abstract: Human-aligned deep learning models exhibit behaviors consistent with human values, such as robustness, fairness, and honesty. Transferring these behavioral properties to models trained on different tasks or data distributions remains challenging: aligned behavior is easily forgotten during fine-tuning, and collecting task-specific data that preserves this behavior can be prohibitively costly. We introduce BIRD (Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation), a flexible framework for transferring aligned behavior by matching the internal representation structure of a student model to that of a teacher. Applied to out-of-distribution robustness in image classification, BIRD outperforms fine-tuning, transfer learning, and continual learning methods, improving robust accuracy by up to 16% over the next strongest baseline. It remains effective even when the teacher is trained on a much simpler dataset and is $25 \times$ smaller than the student. In a large-scale study of over 400 teacher-student pairs, we show that three interpretable and computable properties of the teacher's representations (i.e., task relevance, behavioral relevance, and complementary knowledge) explain up to 85% of the variance in transfer success. These insights offer practical guidance for teacher selection and design. BIRD turns small, well-aligned models into scalable alignment seeds, removing a key bottleneck in deploying safe AI systems in the wild.

papers.title: NeuronTune: Fine-Grained Neuron Modulation for Balanced Safety-Utility Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to achieve a balance between robust safety and utility preservation in Large Language Models (LLMs) by moving beyond coarse-grained layer-wise interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronTune, a fine-grained neuron-level alignment framework that identifies safety-critical and utility-preserving neurons via attack-aware attribution and adaptively modulates them using meta-learning to balance safety and utility.
papers.conclusion: NeuronTune effectively balances robust safety and utility preservation in LLMs through fine-grained neuron modulation and offers a tunable mechanism for flexible adaptation to different application scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Coarse-grained layer-wise interventions inherently trade off safety and utility, leading to exaggerated safety or utility degradation.
NeuronTune outperforms existing methods in balancing safety and utility, achieving higher Safety-Utility F1 (SU-F1) scores across multiple LLMs.
Safety and utility neurons are distributed across all layers, with safety neurons peaking in middle layers and utility neurons concentrated in deeper layers.
The tunable neuron-count regulation mechanism allows adaptation to diverse safety and utility demands by adjusting the number of modulated neurons.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each component: strategic attack selection, neuron pinpointing, and adaptive adjustment.
papers.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment while preserving utility is critical for the reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, current techniques fundamentally suffer from intertwined deficiencies: insufficient robustness against malicious attacks, frequent refusal of benign queries, degradation in generated text quality and general task performance--the former two reflecting deficits in robust safety and the latter constituting utility impairment. We trace these limitations to the coarse-grained layer-wise interventions in existing methods. To resolve this, we propose NeuronTune, a fine-grained framework that dynamically modulates sparse neurons to achieve simultaneous safety-utility optimization. Our approach first identifies safety-critical and utility-preserving neurons across all layers via attribution, then employs meta-learning to adaptively amplify safety-neuron activations and suppress utility-neuron activations. Crucially, NeuronTune enables tunable adjustment of intervention scope via neuron-count thresholds, supporting flexible adaptation to security-critical or utility-priority scenarios. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art technologies, achieving superior model safety while maintaining excellent utility.

papers.title: TRACEALIGN -- Tracing the Drift: Attributing Alignment Failures to Training-Time Belief Sources in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the training-time belief sources underlying alignment failures in LLMs, and how can we trace and mitigate them?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TRACE ALIGN, a unified framework that traces unsafe LLM completions back to their root causes in the training corpus via span-level provenance and a Belief Conflict Index (BCI), enabling effective interventions to reduce alignment drift.
papers.conclusion: TRACE ALIGN transforms alignment from a surface behavioral endeavor into a mechanistic, traceable process grounded in epistemic provenance, providing a scalable toolkit for understanding and mitigating alignment failures at their source.
papers.key_findings:
The TRACE ALIGN framework reduces alignment drift by up to 85% on the curated Alignment Drift Benchmark (ADB).
The Belief Conflict Index (BCI) effectively quantifies semantic inconsistency between generated spans and aligned policies based on retrieved training documents.
The proposed interventions—TRACE SHIELD (inference-time filter), Contrastive Belief Deconfliction Loss (fine-tuning objective), and Prov-Decode (provenance-aware decoding)—synergistically improve safety while preserving utility.
papers.limitation:
Lexical rigidity of TRACE INDEX: sensitive to surface variations, semantically equivalent but lexically divergent spans may go undetected.
Simplistic token modeling in BCI: uses unigram token probabilities, which may over-penalize rare but benign phrases.
Corpus-scale indexing bottlenecks: scales poorly with massive pretraining corpora.
Temporal blindness to alignment phase: does not distinguish whether a belief came from pretraining or alignment fine-tuning.
Subjectivity in human evaluation: belief-to-span causal validity remains unverified.
Applicability to closed-source models: relies on span-level access to training data, limiting direct use with proprietary models.
future_direction: Differentiable alignment attribution, where BCI becomes a regularized loss in contrastive fine-tuning.
Instruction-retargeting defenses, where belief traces generate minimal adversarial perturbations to test robustness.
Multi-modal extensions, applying TRACE ALIGN to vision-language models where grounding spans include image regions and captions.
Live memory audits, akin to interpretability dashboards, where each refusal is explainable via retrieved spans.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) fine-tuned to align with human values often exhibit alignment drift, producing unsafe or policy-violating completions when exposed to adversarial prompts, decoding perturbations, or paraphrased jailbreaks. While prior work has behaviorally characterized alignment failure, little is known about the training-time belief sources underlying these failures. We introduce TraceAlign, a unified framework for tracing unsafe completions back to their root causes in the model's training corpus. Central to our approach is the Belief Conflict Index (BCI), which quantifies semantic inconsistency between generated spans and aligned policies, based on retrieved training documents using suffix-array matching. We propose three complementary interventions: (i) TraceShield, an inference-time safety filter that refuses completions with high-BCI spans, (ii) Contrastive Belief Deconfliction Loss, a contrastive fine-tuning objective penalizing high-BCI continuations during DPO, and (iii) Prov-Decode, a provenance-aware decoding strategy that vetoes beam expansions predicted to yield high-BCI spans. Together, these defenses reduce alignment drift by up to 85% on our curated Alignment Drift Benchmark (ADB) while preserving utility on standard tasks, with delta less than 0.2 and improved refusal quality. We further derive a theoretical upper bound on drift likelihood via suffix-array span statistics, linking memorization frequency and length to adversarial reactivation risk. TraceAlign thus provides the first scalable, traceable, and grounded toolkit for understanding and mitigating alignment failures at source. To encourage further exploration and development, we open-source our implementation at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/tracealign-2DA7

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
papers.research_question: Are the solutions learned by LoRA and full fine-tuning equivalent, and what structural differences exist between them?
papers.core_contribution: LoRA and full fine-tuning learn structurally different solutions: LoRA introduces high-ranking intruder dimensions (new singular vectors) that cause forgetting of pre-training knowledge, and scaling these dimensions reduces forgetting with minimal impact on downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: LoRA and full fine-tuning are not equivalent; intruder dimensions in LoRA cause forgetting and their accumulation harms continual learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA introduces intruder dimensions (new singular vectors) in weight matrices, while full fine-tuning does not.
Intruder dimensions are causally responsible for forgetting of pre-training knowledge.
Scaling down intruder dimensions reduces forgetting with minimal drop in downstream task performance.
LoRA generally forgets less than full fine-tuning, but this depends on hyperparameters (alpha and learning rate); with certain settings, LoRA can forget more.
In continual learning, LoRA accumulates intruder dimensions and forgets previously learned tasks more than full fine-tuning.
future_direction: Rigorous analysis of all possible LoRA variants.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning is a crucial paradigm for adapting pre-trained large language models to downstream tasks. Recently, methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have been shown to effectively fine-tune LLMs with an extreme reduction in trainable parameters. But, \emph{are their learned solutions really equivalent?} We study how LoRA and full-finetuning change pre-trained models by analyzing the model's weight matrices through the lens of their spectral properties. We find that LoRA and full fine-tuning yield weight matrices whose singular value decompositions exhibit very different structure: weight matrices trained with LoRA have new, high-ranking singular vectors, which we call \emph{intruder dimensions}, while those trained with full fine-tuning do not. Further, we extend the finding that LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning and find its forgetting is vastly localized to the intruder dimension -- by causally intervening on the intruder dimensions by changing their associated singular values post-fine-tuning, we show that they cause forgetting. Moreover, scaling them down significantly improves modeling of the pre-training distribution with a minimal drop in downstream task performance. Given this, we should expect accumulating intruder dimensions to be harmful and lead to more forgetting. This will be amplified during continual learning because of sequentially fine-tuning, and we show that LoRA models do accumulate intruder dimensions here tend to perform worse in this setting, emphasizing the practicality of our findings.

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Defenses Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we defend CLIP models against typographic attacks without fine-tuning, by understanding and intervening on the internal mechanisms responsible for typographic vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dyslexify, a gradient-free defense that improves CLIP's robustness to typographic attacks by identifying and ablating a sparse circuit of attention heads responsible for typographic information, without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Dyslexify provides a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient defense against typographic attacks, enabling safer deployment of multimodal models without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specialized attention heads in the latter half of CLIP layers causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token.
Ablating these heads (typographic circuit) improves typographic attack robustness by up to 22.06% on ImageNet-100-typo while standard accuracy drops by less than 1%.
The typographic circuit is sparse, covering at most 10.1% of attention heads.
Dyslexify scales to billion-parameter models and is competitive with fine-tuning-based defenses.
The method effectively mitigates typographic attacks in safety-critical medical foundation models for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Dyslexify only protects the cls token, but many multimodal applications use spatial tokens, allowing typographic information to propagate.
Adaptive attacks are not feasible due to non-differentiability of typographic attacks, so evaluation against adaptive attacks is not possible.
Insights into CLIP's behavior could be misused to craft stronger typographic attacks.
future_direction: Generalizing Dyslexify to VLM setups that use spatial tokens.
papers.abstract: Typographic attacks exploit multi-modal systems by injecting text into images, leading to targeted misclassifications, malicious content generation and even Vision-Language Model jailbreaks. In this work, we analyze how CLIP vision encoders behave under typographic attacks, locating specialized attention heads in the latter half of the model's layers that causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token. Building on these insights, we introduce a method to defend CLIP models against typographic attacks by selectively ablating a typographic circuit, consisting of attention heads. Without requiring finetuning, our method improves performance by up to 19.6% on a typographic variant of ImageNet-100, while reducing standard ImageNet-100 accuracy by less than 1%. Notably, our training-free approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning. To this end, we release a family of dyslexic CLIP models which are significantly more robust against typographic attacks. These models serve as suitable drop-in replacements for a broad range of safety-critical applications, where the risks of text-based manipulation outweigh the utility of text recognition.

papers.title: TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety in large foundation models by intervening at the path level to disconnect causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics, rather than suppressing isolated neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TraceRouter, a path-level safety intervention framework that traces and disconnects causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics in large foundation models, achieving superior adversarial robustness and utility preservation compared to neuron-level methods.
papers.conclusion: TraceRouter provides a robust and interpretable path-level intervention framework for foundation model safety, targeting the topological structure of semantic flow rather than isolated activations.
papers.key_findings:
TraceRouter outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in safety intervention across diffusion models, LLMs, and MLLMs.
Path-level intervention is more effective than neuron-level suppression because harmful semantics are distributed across cross-layer circuits.
TraceRouter preserves general utility (e.g., image fidelity, reasoning capabilities) while ensuring safety.
The identified sensitive pathways are causally validated through amplification experiments, showing they act as switches for harmful generation.
The method is architecture-agnostic and works across diverse model types.
papers.limitation: The framework's applicability to general-purpose tasks beyond safety, such as logical reasoning or creative writing, remains to be fully explored.
future_direction: Validate TraceRouter's path-level intervention across a broader spectrum of non-safety domains.
papers.abstract: Despite their capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current defenses predominantly rely on the "locality hypothesis", suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics act as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering such localized interventions brittle and detrimental to utility. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{TraceRouter}, a path-level framework that traces and disconnects the causal propagation circuits of illicit semantics. TraceRouter operates in three stages: (1) it pinpoints a sensitive onset layer by analyzing attention divergence; (2) it leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and differential activation analysis to disentangle and isolate malicious features; and (3) it maps these features to downstream causal pathways via feature influence scores (FIS) derived from zero-out interventions. By selectively suppressing these causal chains, TraceRouter physically severs the flow of harmful information while leaving orthogonal computation routes intact. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraceRouter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a superior trade-off between adversarial robustness and general utility. Our code will be publicly released. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Alignment Via Interpretability: Layerwise Counterfactuals To Detect Maladaptive Llm Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can layerwise counterfactual interventions on internal representations detect maladaptive behaviors in large language models that are not reliably exposed through prompt-based evaluation alone?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a layerwise counterfactual interpretability framework that detects maladaptive behaviors in LLMs by performing causal interventions on internal representations, demonstrating that intermediate layers encode decision-critical features for alignment.
papers.conclusion: The layerwise counterfactual framework enables proactive detection of alignment risks by revealing internal representations causally linked to maladaptive behaviors, positioning interpretability as a diagnostic tool for safety.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently show the highest causal influence on alignment behavior, often flipping responses between refusal and compliance.
Counterfactual interventions can induce maladaptive behaviors even when baseline outputs appear aligned, revealing latent misalignment.
Layerwise sensitivity patterns are stable across different model checkpoints and random seeds.
Early layers encode surface linguistic features with minimal impact on alignment decisions.
Late layers modulate stylistic aspects of responses rather than core decision outcomes.
papers.limitation:
Counterfactual interventions establish causal influence but do not directly reveal how misalignment features are learned during training.
The analysis focuses on decoder-only transformer architectures, and findings may not fully generalize to other model families or multimodal systems.
Behavioral evaluation metrics, though carefully designed, cannot exhaustively capture all forms of maladaptive behavior.
Interpretability methods may miss distributed or nonlinear representations that do not localize cleanly within individual layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to larger models, multimodal architectures, and training time interventions.
Integrating counterfactual diagnostics into alignment training loops.
Formalizing metrics for internal alignment robustness.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language model alignment remains fragile under distribution shift, jailbreak prompts, and latent goal misgeneralization, motivating the need for diagnostic tools that move beyond surface level behavior to internal representations. This paper investigates alignment via interpretability by introducing a layerwise counterfactual analysis framework that probes how targeted interventions on hidden states alter downstream model behavior. Using publicly available transformer based language models and open interpretability tooling, we perform controlled counterfactual substitutions and activation patching across layers to detect maladaptive behaviors that are not reliably exposed through prompt based evaluation alone. Our analysis demonstrates that specific intermediate layers encode decision critical features whose perturbation consistently induces alignment failures such as reward hacking tendencies, deceptive compliance, and instruction misgeneralization, even when input level behavior appears aligned. We further show that these internal signatures are stable across random seeds and model checkpoints, enabling reproducible detection of misalignment risks prior to deployment. The findings support the thesis that interpretability driven diagnostics can serve as an early warning mechanism for alignment failures and provide a principled foundation for integrating internal model transparency into safety evaluation pipelines.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Alignment: Rebuilding LLMs Safety Mechanism via Probabilistically Ablating Refusal Direction
