However, prior studies have shown that IFT can significantly compromise LLMs' safety, particularly their ability to refuse malicious instructions, raising significant concerns. Recent research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs has identified the refusal direction (r-direction) in the hidden states, which plays a pivotal role in governing refusal behavior. Building on this insight, our study reveals that the r-direction tends to drift during training, which we identify as one of the causes of the associated safety risks. To mitigate such drift, our proposed ProCon method introduces a projection-constrained loss term that regularizes the projection magnitude of each training sample's hidden state onto the r-direction. Our initial analysis shows that applying an appropriate constraint can effectively mitigate the refusal direction drift and associated safety risks, but remains limited by overall performance barriers. To overcome this barrier, informed by our observation of early-stage sharp drift and a data-driven perspective, we introduce a warm-up strategy that emphasizes early-stage strong constraints and broaden the data distribution to strengthen constraint signals, leading to an enhanced ProCon method. Experimental results under various datasets, scenarios, and LLMs demonstrate that our method can significantly mitigate safety risks posed by IFT while preserving task performance gains. Even compared with strong baselines, our method consistently delivers superior overall performance. Crucially, our analysis indicates that ProCon can contribute to stabilizing the r-direction during training, while such an interpretability-driven exploration of LLMs' internal mechanisms lays a solid foundation for future safety research.

papers.title: Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications
papers.research_question: What is the brittleness of safety alignment in large language models, and can it be explained by sparse safety-critical regions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that safety-critical regions in aligned LLMs are sparse and can be isolated via neuron and rank attribution methods, leading to brittleness in safety mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The brittleness of safety alignment stems from sparse safety-critical regions, highlighting the need for more robust safety strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-critical neurons and ranks are sparse, comprising about 3% and 2.5% respectively.
Removing these regions compromises safety while preserving utility.
Models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks even when safety-critical regions are frozen.
Pruning least safety-relevant neurons can enhance safety against adversarial attacks.
Disentanglement methods (set difference and orthogonal projection) effectively isolate safety-critical regions.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to remove safety guardrails from models.
future_direction: Development of more robust safety alignment algorithms that integrate safety-critical regions seamlessly with utility regions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show inherent brittleness in their safety mechanisms, as evidenced by their susceptibility to jailbreaking and even non-malicious fine-tuning. This study explores this brittleness of safety alignment by leveraging pruning and low-rank modifications. We develop methods to identify critical regions that are vital for safety guardrails, and that are disentangled from utility-relevant regions at both the neuron and rank levels. Surprisingly, the isolated regions we find are sparse, comprising about $3\%$ at the parameter level and $2.5\%$ at the rank level. Removing these regions compromises safety without significantly impacting utility, corroborating the inherent brittleness of the model's safety mechanisms. Moreover, we show that LLMs remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted. These findings underscore the urgent need for more robust safety strategies in LLMs.

papers.title: Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cross-lingual safety alignment in LLMs, specifically identifying a sparse set of shared safety neurons that regulate safety behavior across languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a sparse set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons) that regulate safety behavior across languages and proposes a neuron-oriented training strategy that selectively fine-tunes these neurons to improve safety in low-resource languages without degrading general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cross-lingual safety alignment can be achieved by identifying and selectively fine-tuning a sparse set of shared safety neurons, which improves safety in low-resource languages while minimizing the alignment tax.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) that are causally responsible for safety refusal behavior.
The subset of MS-Neurons shared between high-resource and low-resource languages (SS-Neurons) serves as a bridge for cross-lingual safety transfer.
Suppressing SS-Neurons causes concurrent safety drops across low-resource languages, while reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency.
The proposed SS-Neuron expansion strategy, which fine-tunes only the English MS-Neurons using parallel safety data, significantly reduces attack success rates in low-resource languages while preserving model utility.
The method is parameter-efficient, updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and outperforms state-of-the-art safety alignment methods.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on safety-oriented tasks, and the applicability to general-purpose tasks remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validate the neuron-level intervention across non-safety domains to transfer complex cognitive skills.
papers.abstract: Multilingual safety remains significantly imbalanced, leaving non-high-resource (NHR) languages vulnerable compared to robust high-resource (HR) ones. Moreover, the neural mechanisms driving safety alignment remain unclear despite observed cross-lingual representation transfer. In this paper, we find that LLMs contain a set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons), a remarkably small yet critical neuronal subset that jointly regulates safety behavior across languages. We first identify monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) and validate their causal role in safety refusal behavior through targeted activation and suppression. Our cross-lingual analyses then identify SS-Neurons as the subset of MS-Neurons shared between HR and NHR languages, serving as a bridge to transfer safety capabilities from HR to NHR domains. We observe that suppressing these neurons causes concurrent safety drops across NHR languages, whereas reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency. Building on these insights, we propose a simple neuron-oriented training strategy that targets SS-Neurons based on language resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning this tiny neuronal subset outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly enhancing NHR safety while maintaining the model's general capabilities. The code and dataset will be available athttps://github.com/1518630367/SS-Neuron-Expansion.

papers.title: LSSF: Safety Alignment for Large Language Models through Low-Rank Safety Subspace Fusion
papers.research_question: How to effectively restore safety alignment of fine-tuned large language models without significantly impacting their downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LSSF, a post-hoc safety re-alignment framework that uses low-rank projection to extract and fuse safety principal components, effectively restoring safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal impact on downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: LSSF restores safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs by correcting safety drift within a low-rank subspace, without compromising downstream task performance. The method is architecture-agnostic and plans to extend to multimodal and MoE models.
papers.key_findings:
LSSF effectively restores safety alignment in fine-tuned models across various tasks and model sizes.
The low-rank safety subspace of LLMs is stable during fine-tuning and isolated from general capability directions.
The proposed safety singular value entropy metric quantifies safety information density and helps determine appropriate pruning ranks.
LSSF outperforms baseline methods in balancing safety restoration and utility preservation.
The method is robust to different proportions of harmful/safe data in the fine-tuning dataset.
papers.limitation: Budget constraints prevented evaluation on larger models like Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct.
future_direction: Extend the method to multimodal and mixture of experts (MoE) models.
papers.abstract: The safety mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) exhibit notable fragility, as even fine-tuning on datasets without harmful content may still undermine their safety capabilities. Meanwhile, existing safety alignment methods predominantly rely on the fine-tuning process, which inadvertently leads to the increased complexity and computational resources required. To address these issues, we introduce LSSF, a novel safety re-alignment framework with \underline{L}ow-Rank \underline{S}afety \underline{S}ubspace \underline{F}usion. Our proposed method exploits the low-rank characteristics of safety information in LLMs by constructing a low-rank projection matrix to extract the principal components of safety vectors. Notably, this projection matrix represents the low-rank safety subspace of the LLMs, which we have observed to remain stable during fine-tuning process and is isolated from the model's general capabilities. These principal components are used to effectively restore safety alignment when combined with fine-tuned LLMs through linear arithmetic. Additionally, to account for the varying encoding densities of safety information across different layers of LLMs, we propose a novel metric called safety singular value entropy. This metric quantifies the encoding density and allows for the dynamic computation of the safety-critical rank for each safety vector. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed post-hoc alignment method can effectively restore the safety alignment of fine-tuned models with minimal impact on their performance in downstream tasks.

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators. This supervision enables the VAE to learn disentangled latent representations that capture distinct adversarial characteristics while maintaining semantic interpretability. Through targeted manipulation of learned latent dimensions, LATENTGUARD achieves selective refusal behavior, effectively blocking harmful requests while preserving helpfulness for legitimate use cases. Experiments on Qwen3-8B demonstrate significant improvements in both safety controllability and response interpretability without compromising utility. Cross-architecture validation on Mistral-7B confirms the generalizability of our latent steering approach, showing consistent effectiveness across different model families. Our results suggest that structured representation-level intervention offers a promising pathway toward building safer yet practical LLM systems.

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.research_question: What is the reason for safety alignment drop after LoRA fine-tuning, and how can we preserve safety alignment during low-rank adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SaLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves safety alignment by introducing a fixed safety module and task-specific initialization for low-rank adapters.
papers.conclusion: SaLoRA effectively preserves safety alignment during LoRA fine-tuning while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning significantly alters the safety features of LLMs, leading to a drop in safety alignment.
SaLoRA, with its fixed safety module and task-specific initialization, preserves safety alignment while achieving comparable or better downstream task performance.
SaLoRA outperforms existing PEFT methods (LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA) and post-hoc alignment methods (Self-Reminder, InferAligner, Vaccine, Safe LoRA) in terms of harmful rate and utility.
Task-specific initialization for SaLoRA adapters improves convergence and performance compared to standard initialization.
SaLoRA maintains safety alignment even under jailbreak attacks (multi-GCG attack).
papers.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: How Does DPO Reduce Toxicity? A Mechanistic Neuron-Level Analysis
papers.research_question: How does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) reduce toxicity in language models? The paper investigates whether the prior explanation (dampening toxic neurons) is complete and seeks a more comprehensive mechanism.
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity through distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, balancing opposing effects, not just by dampening a few 'toxic' neurons. The paper introduces an activation editing method that mimics this effect without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a more complete mechanistic understanding of DPO's toxicity reduction via distributed activation shifts and introduces an efficient, training-free alternative through activation editing.
papers.key_findings:
Toxic neurons (identified by toxic token projection) account for only 2.5% to 24% of DPO's toxicity reduction effect across models.
DPO induces distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons, with roughly half reducing and half increasing their projection onto a toxicity direction, leading to a net reduction.
Four neuron groups (toxic-aligned positive, toxic-aligned negative, anti-toxic-aligned positive, anti-toxic-aligned negative) are identified, whose combined activation shifts replicate DPO's effect.
Activation patching of these four groups matches or exceeds the toxicity reduction achieved by DPO.
The proposed activation editing method, which applies small, distributed shifts to neuron activations based on their alignment to a toxicity representation, outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring weight updates.
papers.limitation:
Using a linear probe captures toxicity as a single direction, but toxicity may be better represented as a subspace capturing different aspects (e.g., hate speech, abusive language).
The projection method assumes neurons contribute proportionally along their activated directions, but toxicity representations may be distributed across more complex linear combinations of neurons.
The four neuron groups and activation editing method are demonstrated for toxicity reduction; generalizing them to other binary safety tasks (e.g., bias, misinformation) or to general instruction-tuned models requires future work.
future_direction: More robust analysis of toxic subspace projections instead of a single direction.
Extending the four neuron groups analysis to other binary safety-related tasks trained with DPO (e.g., biased vs. unbiased content).
Extending the activation editing method to other safety-related tasks or general tasks where a linear concept representation can be derived.
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning algorithms reduce harmful outputs in language models, yet their mechanisms remain under-explored. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a popular choice of algorithm, but prior explanations, attributing its effects solely to dampened toxic neurons in the MLP layers, are incomplete. In this study, we analyse four language models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B, Mistral-7B, GPT-2-Medium) and show that toxic neurons only account for 2.5% to 24% of DPO's effects across models. Instead, DPO balances distributed activation shifts across all MLP neurons to create a net toxicity reduction. We attribute this reduction to four neuron groups, two aligned with reducing toxicity and two promoting anti-toxicity, whose combined effects replicate DPO across models. To further validate this understanding, we develop an activation editing method mimicking DPO through distributed shifts along a toxicity representation. This method outperforms DPO in reducing toxicity while preserving perplexity, without requiring any weight updates. Our work provides a mechanistic understanding of DPO and introduces an efficient, tuning-free alternative for safety fine-tuning.

papers.title: SEAL: Systematic Error Analysis for Value ALignment
papers.research_question: How well do reward models learn and align with human values from alignment datasets, and what causes alignment resistance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SEAL methodology with metrics to evaluate value alignment in RLHF, revealing significant feature imprints and alignment resistance in reward models.
papers.conclusion: The study underscores the need for detailed analyses of reward models and alignment datasets to better understand and address limitations in RLHF methodologies.
papers.key_findings:
Feature imprint shows that reward models significantly learn target features like harmlessness and helpfulness.
Alignment resistance occurs in 26% of the dataset where the reward model disagrees with human preferences.
Misalignment often arises from ambiguous entries in the alignment dataset.
Reward models are sensitive to spoiler features, with rewriting to positive tone increasing misalignment.
The LM-labeler and reward model sometimes agree to disagree with human labels, indicating shared interpretation.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on LM-labelers for featurization, which may introduce instability and lack ground truth.
Lack of systematic identification and definition of spoiler features across different contexts.
future_direction: Studying alignment resistance on semantic tasks like web-gpt and summarize-from-feedback.
Developing better open-source alignment pipelines with high-quality taxonomy labels.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aims to align language models (LMs) with human values by training reward models (RMs) on binary preferences and using these RMs to fine-tune the base LMs. Despite its importance, the internal mechanisms of RLHF remain poorly understood. This paper introduces new metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of modeling and aligning human values, namely feature imprint, alignment resistance and alignment robustness. We categorize alignment datasets into target features (desired values) and spoiler features (undesired concepts). By regressing RM scores against these features, we quantify the extent to which RMs reward them - a metric we term feature imprint. We define alignment resistance as the proportion of the preference dataset where RMs fail to match human preferences, and we assess alignment robustness by analyzing RM responses to perturbed inputs. Our experiments, utilizing open-source components like the Anthropic/hh-rlhf preference dataset and OpenAssistant RMs, reveal significant imprints of target features and a notable sensitivity to spoiler features. We observed a 26% incidence of alignment resistance in portions of the dataset where LM-labelers disagreed with human preferences. Furthermore, we find that misalignment often arises from ambiguous entries within the alignment dataset. These findings underscore the importance of scrutinizing both RMs and alignment datasets for a deeper understanding of value alignment.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Revisiting Robustness for LLM Safety Alignment via Selective Geometry Control
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether robustness failures in LLM safety alignment can be addressed by data-centric methods alone, and proposes a geometry-aware optimization framework to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that selectively stabilizes safety-critical parameter directions to improve robustness under domain shift and noisy supervision.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that optimization geometry is a complementary axis for robust LLM safety alignment, and ShaPO effectively improves robustness by selectively stabilizing safety-critical parameter directions.
papers.key_findings:
ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings.
ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains.
Selective geometry control avoids over-regularization and improves cross-domain robustness compared to uniform control.
Token-level and reward-level ShaPO both improve robustness, with reward-level ShaPO offering additional stability under noisy supervision.
Perturbing a small fraction of safety-critical neurons accounts for most of the worst-case alignment loss, justifying selective control.
papers.limitation:
ShaPO introduces additional computational overhead due to geometry-aware optimization.
Identification of alignment-critical directions is based on approximate signals (linear probe).
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of geometry-aware optimization for larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models remains brittle under domain shift and noisy preference supervision. Most existing robust alignment methods focus on uncertainty in alignment data, while overlooking optimization-induced fragility in preference-based objectives. In this work, we revisit robustness for LLM safety alignment from an optimization geometry perspective, and argue that robustness failures cannot be addressed by data-centric methods alone. We propose ShaPO, a geometry-aware preference optimization framework that enforces worst-case alignment objectives via selective geometry control over alignment-critical parameter subspace. By avoiding uniform geometry constraints, ShaPO mitigates the over-regularization that can harm robustness under distribution shift. We instantiate ShaPO at two levels: token-level ShaPO stabilizes likelihood-based surrogate optimization, while reward-level ShaPO enforces reward-consistent optimization under noisy supervision. Across diverse safety benchmarks and noisy preference settings, ShaPO consistently improves safety robustness over popular preference optimization methods. Moreover, ShaPO composes cleanly with data-robust objectives, yielding additional gains and empirically supporting the proposed optimization-geometry perspective.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: Diagnosing Catastrophe: Large parts of accuracy loss in continual learning can be accounted for by readout misalignment
papers.research_question: What representational changes underlie catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, and what processes account for the performance decrease?
papers.core_contribution: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is largely due to misalignment between hidden representations and readout layers, rather than loss of information in the representations.
papers.conclusion: Information in hidden layers is largely preserved during continual learning, and catastrophic forgetting may be efficiently addressed by solving readout misalignment without restricting learning of new tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Performance degradation in continual learning is primarily caused by readout misalignment, not by loss of task-relevant information in hidden representations.
Representational geometry is partially conserved under misalignment, with Procrustes alignment recovering about half of the performance drop.
Only a small fraction of information is irrecoverably lost (true forgetting).
Representational changes (misalignment, geometry change, forgetting) scale with the dimensionality of hidden representations.
Feature transfer from previous tasks contributes to performance on new tasks, but newly learned features provide additional, preserved information.
future_direction: Test the analysis framework for characterizing representational changes in continual learning on biological data.
papers.abstract: Unlike primates, training artificial neural networks on changing data distributions leads to a rapid decrease in performance on old tasks. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we investigate the representational changes that underlie this performance decrease and identify three distinct processes that together account for the phenomenon. The largest component is a misalignment between hidden representations and readout layers. Misalignment occurs due to learning on additional tasks and causes internal representations to shift. Representational geometry is partially conserved under this misalignment and only a small part of the information is irrecoverably lost. All types of representational changes scale with the dimensionality of hidden representations. These insights have implications for deep learning applications that need to be continuously updated, but may also aid aligning ANN models to the rather robust biological vision.

papers.title: SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoder
papers.research_question: Can we interpret reward model decisions? Can we understand the influence of preference data on reward models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFER, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to interpret reward models by extracting safety-relevant features, enabling targeted data manipulation for precise safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: SAFER provides a practical tool for interpreting reward models and performing precise, feature-guided manipulation of preference data, enhancing the transparency and controllability of safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAFER identifies human-interpretable, monosemantic features in reward model activations that are strongly associated with safety.
Using feature-level scores, SAFER enables precise data poisoning that significantly degrades safety alignment with minimal impact on general chat performance.
SAFER also enables effective data denoising, improving safety alignment by removing low-quality preference pairs.
GPT-4o's safety relevance ratings show high alignment with human judgments, validating its use as an automated evaluator.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of safety-oriented fine-tuning and sentence-level representation for effective feature extraction.
papers.limitation:
Generalization to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness) remains an open question.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale models; evaluation on larger models is needed.
future_direction: Explore the application of SAFER to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness).
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a key paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet the reward models at its core remain largely opaque. In this work, we present Sparse Autoencoder For Enhanced Reward model (\textbf{SAFER}), a novel framework for interpreting and improving reward models through mechanistic analysis. Leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we uncover human-interpretable features in reward model activations, enabling insight into safety-relevant decision-making. We apply SAFER to safety-oriented preference datasets and quantify the salience of individual features by activation differences between chosen and rejected responses. Using these feature-level signals, we design targeted data poisoning and denoising strategies. Experiments show that SAFER can precisely degrade or enhance safety alignment with minimal data modification, without sacrificing general chat performance. Our approach contributes to interpreting, auditing and refining reward models in high-stakes LLM alignment tasks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/xzy-101/SAFER-code. \textit{This paper discusses topics related to reward model safety and may include discussions or examples that highlight potential risks or unsafe outcomes.}

papers.title: Understanding and Preserving Safety in Fine-Tuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Why does the safety-utility trade-off become increasingly difficult to maintain as fine-tuning depth increases? Can we leverage the intrinsic training dynamics and geometric properties of updates to achieve a more robust and adaptive safety-utility trade-off?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Preserving Fine-tuning (SPF), a method that removes gradient components conflicting with a low-rank safety subspace during fine-tuning, theoretically guaranteeing utility convergence while bounding safety drift and empirically maintaining safety and utility.
papers.conclusion: SPF provides a mechanistic understanding and practical guidance for always-aligned LLM fine-tuning, effectively preserving safety while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
Safety gradients lie in a low-rank subspace, while utility gradients span a broader high-dimensional space.
Safety and utility subspaces are often negatively correlated, causing directional conflicts during fine-tuning.
The dominant safety direction can be efficiently estimated from a single safety-aligned sample.
SPF consistently maintains downstream task performance and recovers nearly all pre-trained safety alignment, even under adversarial fine-tuning.
SPF exhibits robust resistance to both deep fine-tuning and dynamic jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning is an essential and pervasive functionality for applying large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks. However, it has the potential to substantially degrade safety alignment, e.g., by greatly increasing susceptibility to jailbreak attacks, even when the fine-tuning data is entirely harmless. Despite garnering growing attention in defense efforts during the fine-tuning stage, existing methods struggle with a persistent safety-utility dilemma: emphasizing safety compromises task performance, whereas prioritizing utility typically requires deep fine-tuning that inevitably leads to steep safety declination. In this work, we address this dilemma by shedding new light on the geometric interaction between safety- and utility-oriented gradients in safety-aligned LLMs. Through systematic empirical analysis, we uncover three key insights: (I) safety gradients lie in a low-rank subspace, while utility gradients span a broader high-dimensional space; (II) these subspaces are often negatively correlated, causing directional conflicts during fine-tuning; and (III) the dominant safety direction can be efficiently estimated from a single sample. Building upon these novel insights, we propose safety-preserving fine-tuning (SPF), a lightweight approach that explicitly removes gradient components conflicting with the low-rank safety subspace. Theoretically, we show that SPF guarantees utility convergence while bounding safety drift. Empirically, SPF consistently maintains downstream task performance and recovers nearly all pre-trained safety alignment, even under adversarial fine-tuning scenarios. Furthermore, SPF exhibits robust resistance to both deep fine-tuning and dynamic jailbreak attacks. Together, our findings provide new mechanistic understanding and practical guidance toward always-aligned LLM fine-tuning.

papers.title: Dissecting Fine-Tuning Unlearning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do fine-tuning-based unlearning methods appear successful in behavioral tests, and what is their actual mechanism and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not genuinely erase problematic knowledge; instead, they alter the model's knowledge retrieval process by modifying the coefficients in the MLP's final layers, which also negatively impacts unrelated knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods do not erase knowledge but alter knowledge extraction mechanisms, and they negatively impact the model's unrelated capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Restoring the value vectors in MLPs does not recover unlearned knowledge, indicating that the knowledge remains stored.
Restoring the attention states in intermediate and deeper layers recovers some knowledge, showing that attention components are involved in knowledge extraction.
Restoring the coefficients in the final layers of MLPs recovers most of the unlearned knowledge, indicating that these coefficients are the primary contributors to the unlearning effect.
Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods have a global negative effect, degrading the model's performance on unrelated knowledge.
The unlearning mechanism works by altering the model's knowledge retrieval process rather than erasing the knowledge itself.
papers.limitation: The experiments disregard potential unlearning impact from parameter changes in other model components (e.g., unembedding matrix and normalization layers), and it is unclear if these changes have meaningful effects.
future_direction: Future unlearning evaluations should focus on precise measurement of knowledge storage and retrieval dynamics.
Further investigation into defensive strategies based on the findings about MLP coefficients.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning-based unlearning methods prevail for preventing targeted harmful, sensitive, or copyrighted information within large language models while preserving overall capabilities. However, the true effectiveness of these methods is unclear. In this work, we delve into the limitations of fine-tuning-based unlearning through activation patching and parameter restoration experiments. Our findings reveal that these methods alter the model's knowledge retrieval process, providing further evidence that they do not genuinely erase the problematic knowledge embedded in the model parameters. Instead, the coefficients generated by the MLP components in the model's final layer are the primary contributors to these seemingly positive unlearning effects, playing a crucial role in controlling the model's behaviors. Furthermore, behavioral tests demonstrate that this unlearning mechanism inevitably impacts the global behavior of the models, affecting unrelated knowledge or capabilities. The code is released at https://github.com/yihuaihong/Dissecting-FT-Unlearning.

papers.title: Reviving Your MNEME: Predicting The Side Effects of LLM Unlearning and Fine-Tuning via Sparse Model Diffing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned large language models without access to fine-tuning data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MNEME, a framework that uses sparse model diffing to detect unintended side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs without access to fine-tuning data, achieving high accuracy across multiple scenarios.
papers.conclusion: MNEME is a general-purpose framework that effectively detects side effects in fine-tuned or unlearned LLMs using sparse model diffing, highlighting the promise of scalable, data-agnostic auditing tools.
papers.key_findings:
MNEME achieves up to 95% accuracy in predicting side effects on WMDP unlearning tasks.
On emergent misalignment, MNEME achieves 68.2% accuracy with perfect precision.
In benign fine-tuning scenarios, MNEME shows strong performance with up to 92.9% accuracy.
Sparse model diffing effectively isolates behavioral shifts without requiring fine-tuning data.
Retraining on high-activation samples can partially reverse the detected side effects.
papers.limitation:
Relies on task-agnostic corpora which may not reflect specific fine-tuning distributions.
Interpretability pipeline depends on LLM-generated descriptions, which may introduce noise or imprecision.
Cross-Coder was not originally designed for model diffing, and architectural constraints may limit fine-grained change capture.
Provides correlational insights rather than causal guarantees.
Computationally demanding due to need for model activations and large-scale inference.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are frequently fine-tuned or unlearned to adapt to new tasks or eliminate undesirable behaviors. While existing evaluation methods assess performance after such interventions, there remains no general approach for detecting unintended side effects, such as unlearning biology content degrading performance on chemistry tasks, particularly when these effects are unpredictable or emergent. To address this issue, we introduce MNEME, Model diffiNg for Evaluating Mechanistic Effects, a lightweight framework for identifying these side effects using sparse model diffing. MNEME compares base and fine-tuned models on task-agnostic data (for example, The Pile, LMSYS-Chat-1M) without access to fine-tuning data to isolate behavioral shifts. Applied to five LLMs across three scenarios: WMDP knowledge unlearning, emergent misalignment, and benign fine-tuning, MNEME achieves up to 95 percent accuracy in predicting side effects, aligning with known benchmarks and requiring no custom heuristics. Furthermore, we show that retraining on high-activation samples can partially reverse these effects. Our results demonstrate that sparse probing and diffing offer a scalable and automated lens into fine-tuning-induced model changes, providing practical tools for understanding and managing LLM behavior.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does distributional gap in safety alignment datasets cause reasoning degradation (safety tax) in large reasoning models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DGR, a data refinement method that aligns safety datasets with the target model's distribution to mitigate safety tax, and shows that distribution shift correlates with reasoning degradation and that safety alignment acts as a knowledge activation mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Distribution shift induced by safety alignment is a primary driver of reasoning degradation in LRMs; DGR mitigates safety tax by aligning safety data with the model's native distribution, and safety alignment functions as a latent-knowledge activator.
papers.key_findings:
DGR effectively mitigates safety tax, improving average reasoning accuracy by +30.2% on DirectRefusal and +21.2% on R1-ACT compared to Vanilla SFT.
The degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting bridging this gap is central to preserving reasoning capability.
Safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere 10 samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors.
DGR is robust to refinement templates and generalizes to larger model scales (tested on 32B).
Fixed safety templates lead to over-refusal and low lexical diversity, highlighting the need for nuanced safety.
papers.limitation:
Not extending DGR to RL-based safety alignment pipelines.
Limited scaling to massive reasoning models (only tested up to 32B due to computational constraints).
future_direction: Extending DGR to reinforcement learning–based safety alignment pipelines.
More comprehensive evaluations on LRMs with larger parameter scales (e.g., 70B and beyond).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment incurs safety tax that perturbs a large reasoning model's (LRM) general reasoning ability. Existing datasets used for safety alignment for an LRM are usually constructed by distilling safety reasoning traces and answers from an external LRM or human labeler. However, such reasoning traces and answers exhibit a distributional gap with the target LRM that needs alignment, and we conjecture such distributional gap is the culprit leading to significant degradation of reasoning ability of the target LRM. Driven by this hypothesis, we propose a safety alignment dataset construction method, dubbed DGR. DGR transforms and refines an existing out-of-distributional safety reasoning dataset to be aligned with the target's LLM inner distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that i) DGR effectively mitigates the safety tax while maintaining safety performance across all baselines, i.e., achieving \textbf{+30.2\%} on DirectRefusal and \textbf{+21.2\%} on R1-ACT improvement in average reasoning accuracy compared to Vanilla SFT; ii) the degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting that bridging this gap is central to preserving capabilities. Furthermore, we find that safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere \textbf{10} samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors. These findings not only emphasize the importance of distributional consistency but also provide insights into the activation mechanism of safety in reasoning models.

papers.title: BLOCK-EM: Preventing Emergent Misalignment by Blocking Causal Features
papers.research_question: Can emergent misalignment be prevented during fine-tuning by blocking the internal features that causally control it?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BLOCK-EM, a training-time intervention that blocks causally relevant internal features to prevent emergent misalignment during fine-tuning, achieving significant reduction in misalignment while preserving in-domain performance.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our findings show that emergent misalignment can be mitigated via targeted training-time interventions on internal mechanisms, connecting mechanistic interpretability with practical alignment interventions.
papers.key_findings:
BLOCK-EM reduces emergent misalignment by up to 95% relative reduction across six fine-tuning domains.
The method preserves in-domain task performance and generation quality.
The causal features identified are transferable across domains.
Under prolonged fine-tuning, misalignment can re-emerge, suggesting rerouting through alternative features.
Blocking an expanded set of features can further suppress re-emergence.
papers.limitation: Misalignment can re-emerge under prolonged fine-tuning, possibly due to rerouting through alternative features or layers.
future_direction: Interventions covering larger subspace and/or multiple layers to prevent rerouting.
