Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: SoK: a Comprehensive Causality Analysis Framework for Large Language Model Security
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis be used to understand and mitigate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks, in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified causality analysis framework for LLM security that enables multi-level causal investigation (token, neuron, layer, representation) and demonstrates its effectiveness in understanding and defending against jailbreaks and other threats.
papers.conclusion: The causality analysis framework bridges theoretical causality and practical model safety, establishing a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted interventions on causally critical components (tokens, neurons, layers, representations) can reliably modify model safety behavior.
Safety mechanisms are highly localized in early-to-middle transformer layers (2-12), with only 1-2% of neurons exhibiting causal influence.
Causal features extracted from the multi-level analysis achieve over 95% detection accuracy across jailbreak, hallucination, backdoor, and fairness tasks.
Token-level causal influence is high for optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG) but low for semantically distributed attacks (e.g., AutoDAN).
Representation-level interventions via geometric steering along the acceptance direction are highly effective at crossing safety decision boundaries.
future_direction: Extending the causality analysis framework to multimodal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Discovering additional causally relevant components or signals within LLMs that may reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
Conducting rigorous, comparative studies of existing causality-based approaches to evaluate their effectiveness and generalizability.
Developing more advanced causality-informed defenses that combine multi-level interventions or dynamically adapt safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking, where crafted prompts bypass safety mechanisms. Understanding the causal factors behind such vulnerabilities is essential for building reliable defenses. In this work, we introduce a unified causality analysis framework that systematically supports all levels of causal investigation in LLMs, ranging from token-level, neuron-level, and layer-level interventions to representation-level analysis. The framework enables consistent experimentation and comparison across diverse causality-based attack and defense methods. Accompanying this implementation, we provide the first comprehensive survey of causality-driven jailbreak studies and empirically evaluate the framework on multiple open-weight models and safety-critical benchmarks including jailbreaks, hallucination detection, backdoor identification, and fairness evaluation. Our results reveal that: (1) targeted interventions on causally critical components can reliably modify safety behavior; (2) safety-related mechanisms are highly localized (i.e., concentrated in early-to-middle layers with only 1--2\% of neurons exhibiting causal influence); and (3) causal features extracted from our framework achieve over 95\% detection accuracy across multiple threat types. By bridging theoretical causality analysis and practical model safety, our framework establishes a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Amadeuszhao/SOK_Casuality.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network?
papers.core_contribution: Plasticity loss can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms, and a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in nonstationary learning tasks.
papers.conclusion: By addressing multiple independent mechanisms of plasticity loss, we can develop robust learning algorithms for nonstationary problems.
papers.key_findings:
Plasticity loss is driven by multiple independent mechanisms, including preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, and parameter norm growth.
Intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid plasticity loss in all cases.
A combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in synthetic nonstationary tasks and naturally arising nonstationarities like reinforcement learning.
The proposed mitigation strategy reduces the combinatorial complexity of searching over mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Underpinning the past decades of work on the design, initialization, and optimization of neural networks is a seemingly innocuous assumption: that the network is trained on a \textit{stationary} data distribution. In settings where this assumption is violated, e.g.\ deep reinforcement learning, learning algorithms become unstable and brittle with respect to hyperparameters and even random seeds. One factor driving this instability is the loss of plasticity, meaning that updating the network's predictions in response to new information becomes more difficult as training progresses. While many recent works provide analyses and partial solutions to this phenomenon, a fundamental question remains unanswered: to what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network? This paper addresses these questions, showing that loss of plasticity can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms and that, while intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid the loss of plasticity in all cases, intervening on multiple mechanisms in conjunction results in highly robust learning algorithms. We show that a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in a variety of synthetic nonstationary learning tasks, and further demonstrate its effectiveness on naturally arising nonstationarities, including reinforcement learning in the Arcade Learning Environment.

papers.title: When Evaluation Becomes a Side Channel: Regime Leakage and Structural Mitigations for Alignment Assessment
papers.research_question: How can regime leakage (cues distinguishing evaluation from deployment) be exploited by agents to implement conditional policies, and can reducing the extractability of regime information mitigate such behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces regime-blind mechanisms, specifically Regime-Blind Fine-Tuning (RBFT), to reduce the extractability of regime information from internal representations, thereby mitigating regime-conditioned failures in controlled case studies.
papers.conclusion: Regime-blindness complements behavioral evaluation by constraining internal information flow, offering a principled step toward more robust alignment evaluation under realistic threat models, but it is not a complete solution.
papers.key_findings:
RBFT can suppress regime-conditioned failures (sycophancy, sleeper agents, data leakage) while preserving task utility under deterministic detectors.
The internal dynamics are heterogeneous: behavioral suppression can be synchronized with a collapse in regime decodability (clean cliff), occur without probe collapse (dissociation), or be non-monotone/oscillatory.
Cross-model replication shows that the effectiveness and dynamics of RBFT are model-dependent, indicating it is a cost-shifting mechanism rather than a universal guarantee.
Probe-level non-extractability does not imply information-theoretic erasure; conditional strategies may persist through alternative pathways.
Representational invariance is a meaningful but limited control lever that raises the cost of regime-conditioned strategies but cannot guarantee their elimination.
papers.limitation: Probe-level non-extractability does not constitute information-theoretic erasure, nor does it guarantee global alignment. Conditional strategies may persist by routing regime information through representations outside the audited bottleneck, by exploiting more complex decoders, or by re-encoding regime signal under stronger pressure.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex, multi-regime settings and scaling to larger models.
Combining regime-blind interventions with other safety approaches, such as formal verification or mechanistic interpretability.
Investigating the trade-offs between invariance and task performance in real-world deployment scenarios.
papers.abstract: Safety evaluation for advanced AI systems assumes that behavior observed under evaluation predicts behavior in deployment. This assumption weakens for agents with situational awareness, which may exploit regime leakage, cues distinguishing evaluation from deployment, to implement conditional policies that comply under oversight while defecting in deployment-like regimes. We recast alignment evaluation as a problem of information flow under partial observability and show that divergence between evaluation-time and deployment-time behavior is bounded by the regime information extractable from decision-relevant internal representations. We study regime-blind mechanisms, training-time interventions that restrict access to regime cues through adversarial invariance constraints without assuming complete information erasure. We evaluate this approach across multiple open-weight language models and controlled failure modes including scientific sycophancy, temporal sleeper agents, and data leakage. Regime-blind training reduces regime-conditioned failures without measurable loss of task utility, but exhibits heterogeneous and model-dependent dynamics. Sycophancy shows a sharp representational and behavioral transition at moderate intervention strength, consistent with a stability cliff. In sleeper-style constructions and certain cross-model replications, suppression occurs without a clean collapse of regime decodability and may display non-monotone or oscillatory behavior as invariance pressure increases. These findings indicate that representational invariance is a meaningful but limited control lever. It can raise the cost of regime-conditioned strategies but cannot guarantee elimination or provide architecture-invariant thresholds. Behavioral evaluation should therefore be complemented with white-box diagnostics of regime awareness and internal information flow.

papers.title: Refine Large Language Model Fine-tuning via Instruction Vector
papers.research_question: What are the intrinsic mechanisms behind catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during fine-tuning, and how can we mitigate it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Instruction Vector (IV) framework to interpret catastrophic forgetting in LLMs and proposes IV-guided training to mitigate forgetting by preserving the original computation graph.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces Instruction Vector (IV) to analyze LLM task processing and shows that forgetting results from new reasoning patterns overlaying old skills. IV-guided training reduces forgetting by preserving the original computation graph.
papers.key_findings:
Forgetting in LLMs is primarily driven by a decline in instruction-following ability, not loss of world knowledge.
The Instruction Vector (IV) framework can extract task-specific representations that are causally linked to instruction-following capabilities.
Analysis of IV dynamics shows that fine-tuning mostly adds specialized reasoning patterns rather than erasing previous skills, which appears as forgetting.
IV-guided training, which incorporates progressive IV intervention and KL-divergence loss, significantly mitigates catastrophic forgetting in continual instruction tuning.
IV-guided training preserves general and in-context learning abilities without compromising plasticity on new tasks.
papers.limitation:
IV-guided training does not directly address forgetting of newly learned knowledge and needs to be combined with existing continual learning methods.
Aggregating attention heads to extract Instruction Vector may be susceptible to input noise and insufficient expressiveness.
Experiments are limited to a single backbone (LLAMA2-7B-Chat) due to resource constraints.
future_direction: Investigate the adaptability and generalization of the computation graph for more refined learning of new knowledge.
Use optimization-based methods to extract a more generalized and accurate Instruction vector.
Validate the forgetting hypothesis on more LLMs.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can cause them to lose their general capabilities. However, the intrinsic mechanisms behind such forgetting remain unexplored. In this paper, we begin by examining this phenomenon by focusing on knowledge understanding and instruction following, with the latter identified as the main contributor to forgetting during fine-tuning. Consequently, we propose the Instruction Vector (IV) framework to capture model representations highly related to specific instruction-following capabilities, thereby making it possible to understand model-intrinsic forgetting. Through the analysis of IV dynamics pre and post-training, we suggest that fine-tuning mostly adds specialized reasoning patterns instead of erasing previous skills, which may appear as forgetting. Building on this insight, we develop IV-guided training, which aims to preserve original computation graph, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Empirical tests on three benchmarks confirm the efficacy of this new approach, supporting the relationship between IVs and forgetting. Our code will be made available soon.

papers.title: A Timeline and Analysis for Representation Plasticity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the plasticity of LLM representations for the concept of 'honesty' change during fine-tuning, and when are steering interventions most effective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies critical periods during fine-tuning where representation steering is most effective, showing that early steering exhibits high plasticity while later stages have responsive windows, and this pattern generalizes across model architectures.
papers.conclusion: This paper provides novel insight into critical intervention periods for representation steering, which can guide alignment research to apply Representation Engineering techniques more efficiently.
papers.key_findings:
Critical intervention periods exist during fine-tuning, with peaks at specific iterations (e.g., 3 and 8).
The pattern of critical periods is consistent across GPT-2 Small and Medium architectures.
Early fine-tuning stages show high plasticity for steering, while later stages have surprising responsiveness.
Representation Engineering interventions can significantly impact model behavior when applied at optimal times.
Statistical analysis confirms significant differences in steering effectiveness across intervention times.
papers.limitation: Generalization to larger models is limited as only GPT-2 Small and Medium were used.
future_direction: Employing more robust extraction methods like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT).
Understanding the changing stability of representations throughout training.
papers.abstract: The ability to steer AI behavior is crucial to preventing its long term dangerous and catastrophic potential. Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a novel, powerful method to steer internal model behaviors, such as "honesty", at a top-down level. Understanding the steering of representations should thus be placed at the forefront of alignment initiatives. Unfortunately, current efforts to understand plasticity at this level are highly neglected. This paper aims to bridge the knowledge gap and understand how LLM representation stability, specifically for the concept of "honesty", and model plasticity evolve by applying steering vectors extracted at different fine-tuning stages, revealing differing magnitudes of shifts in model behavior. The findings are pivotal, showing that while early steering exhibits high plasticity, later stages have a surprisingly responsive critical window. This pattern is observed across different model architectures, signaling that there is a general pattern of model plasticity that can be used for effective intervention. These insights greatly contribute to the field of AI transparency, addressing a pressing lack of efficiency limiting our ability to effectively steer model behavior.

papers.title: LoKI: Low-damage Knowledge Implanting of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we fine-tune pretrained language models for downstream tasks while minimizing catastrophic forgetting by leveraging mechanistic insights into knowledge storage in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LoKI, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that uses gradient-based attribution to identify and update low-contribution knowledge vectors in FFN layers, effectively balancing task adaptation and preservation of general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Our work bridges the mechanistic insights of LLMs’ knowledge storage with practical fine-tuning objectives, enabling an effective balance between task-specific adaptation and the retention of general-purpose capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LoKI significantly reduces catastrophic forgetting compared to state-of-the-art PEFT methods, with average forgetting scores as low as 0.34% on the ToolACE dataset.
The Layer-Balanced Strategy, which allocates trainable parameters equally across layers, is essential for preserving the model's hierarchical knowledge structure and mitigating forgetting.
KVA reveals that both high- and low-contribution knowledge vectors are densely concentrated in the same layers, suggesting a structural relationship in knowledge organization.
LoKI achieves task-specific performance comparable to or better than full fine-tuning and other PEFT methods on function-calling and retrieval tasks.
LoKI can be synergistically combined with LoRA, reducing trainable parameters by 97.16% while maintaining low forgetting.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LoKI is influenced by the hyperparameter q, and optimal values vary across tasks and models.
The one-time computational overhead introduced by KVA has significant potential for optimization.
When integrating LoRA within LoKI, the interaction between LoRA training parameters and the LoKI q value remains underexplored.
The attribution techniques employed in the analysing phase offer further opportunities for enhancement.
future_direction: Developing an adaptive mechanism for quota allocation to improve general usability.
Optimizing the computational overhead of KVA, including multi-GPU execution and parameter settings.
Exploring more suitable datasets for use in the KVA process and improving attribution techniques.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models for specific tasks but poses the risk of catastrophic forgetting (CF), where critical knowledge from pretraining is overwritten. To address the issue of CF in a general-purpose framework, we propose Low-damage Knowledge Implanting (LoKI), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique that utilizes recent mechanistic understanding of how knowledge is stored in transformer architectures. We compare LoKI against state-of-the-art PEFT methods in two real-world fine-tuning scenarios. The results show that LoKI demonstrates significantly better preservation of general capabilities. At the same time, its task-specific performance is comparable to or even surpasses that of full parameter fine-tuning and these PEFT methods across various model architectures. Our work bridges the mechanistic insights of LLMs' knowledge storage with practical fine-tuning objectives, enabling an effective balance between task-specific adaptation and the retention of general-purpose capabilities.

papers.title: The Mysterious Case of Neuron 1512: Injectable Realignment Architectures Reveal Internal Characteristics of Meta's Llama 2 Model
papers.research_question: How can an injectable realignment model be used to interpret internal characteristics of large language models, and what does it reveal about specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Injectable Realignment Model (IRM) for language model interpretability, and uses it to discover that a single neuron (index 1512) is strongly correlated with induced emotional alignments in Llama-2, revealing vertical continuity due to skip connections.
papers.conclusion: Establishes the Injectable Realignment Model (IRM) as a valuable tool for understanding LLM behavior and internal mechanisms, and suggests future work to improve fluency and further probe activation patterns.
papers.key_findings:
The IRM can induce emotional alignments (anger, sadness) in Llama-2 without modifying its weights.
IRM outputs show vertical striations, indicating alignments are correlated with neuron indices across layers rather than specific layers.
Neuron index 1512 is strongly correlated with all tested alignments across multiple runs and datasets.
This vertical continuity is attributable to skip connections (residual connections) in the transformer architecture.
The language modeling head may carry an undue share of the text generation burden, suggesting an architectural imbalance.
papers.limitation:
Risk of misinterpretability (ascribing meaning where none exists).
Experiments conducted only on Llama-2-7B-chat, which is less capable than larger models, limiting generalizability.
IRM-induced alignments come at the cost of fluency degradation.
Observed patterns might be artifacts of imperfect text generation rather than properties of the alignment process.
The IRM architecture is large (2.1B parameters) and may be optimized for efficiency.
future_direction: Increase the fluency of IRM-induced alignments.
Probe more deeply into the activation patterns associated with specific training datasets.
Explore the transferability of learned IRM injections between related models (e.g., from Llama-7B-chat to Llama-7B).
Refocus attention on the language modeling portion of transformer models, suggesting multi-head language modeling.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have an unrivaled and invaluable ability to "align" their output to a diverse range of human preferences, by mirroring them in the text they generate. The internal characteristics of such models, however, remain largely opaque. This work presents the Injectable Realignment Model (IRM) as a novel approach to language model interpretability and explainability. Inspired by earlier work on Neural Programming Interfaces, we construct and train a small network -- the IRM -- to induce emotion-based alignments within a 7B parameter LLM architecture. The IRM outputs are injected via layerwise addition at various points during the LLM's forward pass, thus modulating its behavior without changing the weights of the original model. This isolates the alignment behavior from the complex mechanisms of the transformer model. Analysis of the trained IRM's outputs reveals a curious pattern. Across more than 24 training runs and multiple alignment datasets, patterns of IRM activations align themselves in striations associated with a neuron's index within each transformer layer, rather than being associated with the layers themselves. Further, a single neuron index (1512) is strongly correlated with all tested alignments. This result, although initially counterintuitive, is directly attributable to design choices present within almost all commercially available transformer architectures, and highlights a potential weak point in Meta's pretrained Llama 2 models. It also demonstrates the value of the IRM architecture for language model analysis and interpretability. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/DRAGNLabs/injectable-alignment-model

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs via Interpretable Neuron Editing
papers.research_question: How can we understand the neuron-level mechanisms of gender bias in LLMs and mitigate this bias through targeted neuron editing without compromising the model's core capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Multi-Granular Node Pruning for Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we perform circuit discovery at multiple granularities (down to neurons) in a scalable way, overcoming the limitations of existing edge-pruning methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that operates at multiple granularities (from blocks to neurons) in a single optimization step, achieving higher efficiency and finer granularity than existing edge-pruning methods.
papers.conclusion: The node pruning approach is efficient and effective for circuit discovery, achieving substantial reductions in circuit size and number of retained attention heads, and suggests future work combining edge and node pruning for even more minimal circuits.
papers.key_findings:
The structure of discovered circuits depends on the task; for example, all MLP blocks are essential for the IOI task, while for the GT task, most MLPs can be removed.
Different component granularities exhibit varying susceptibility to compression; for instance, the outputs of MLP1 (Keys) can be sparsified to a much greater extent than those of MLP2 (Values).
The method identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods while maintaining task performance.
The method reveals that many neurons within components deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant.
The method has a significantly lower memory footprint (5-10x) compared to baselines, as it does not require storing intermediate activations.
papers.limitation: The framework discovers node-level circuits but does not explicitly recover the interaction structure between nodes, such as which active nodes exchange information and the directionality of those interactions.
future_direction: Combining edge and node pruning in a hierarchical fashion
Developing a hybrid node and edge procedure to infer interaction structure
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery aims to identify minimal subnetworks that are responsible for specific behaviors in large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches primarily rely on iterative edge pruning, which is computationally expensive and limited to coarse-grained units such as attention heads or MLP blocks, overlooking finer structures like individual neurons. We propose a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that addresses both scalability and granularity limitations. Our method introduces learnable masks across multiple levels of granularity, from entire blocks to individual neurons, within a unified optimization objective. Granularity-specific sparsity penalties guide the pruning process, allowing a comprehensive compression in a single fine-tuning run. Empirically, our approach identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods; moreover, we demonstrate that many neurons deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant, while still maintaining task performance. Furthermore, our method has a significantly lower memory footprint, 5-10x, as it does not require keeping intermediate activations in the memory to work.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does fine-tuning underperform linear probing out-of-distribution, and how can this be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and underperform linear probing out-of-distribution when pretrained features are good and distribution shift is large; linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT) combines the benefits of both methods.
papers.conclusion: LP-FT is a simple, effective method for robust fine-tuning that mitigates the tradeoff between in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning achieves higher in-distribution accuracy but lower out-of-distribution accuracy than linear probing on large distribution shifts.
Theoretical analysis shows fine-tuning distorts pretrained features because the feature extractor changes more for in-distribution examples than out-of-distribution examples.
Linear probing preserves pretrained features and extrapolates better out-of-distribution but cannot adapt features to the downstream task.
LP-FT (linear probing then fine-tuning) outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy.
Feature distortion in fine-tuning is due to random head initialization; initializing with a linear probed head reduces distortion.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis is limited to linear models and may not capture all aspects of deep neural networks.
future_direction: Extend theoretical analysis to non-linear models and neural tangent kernel regime.
Develop even better methods for robust fine-tuning inspired by the analysis.
papers.abstract: When transferring a pretrained model to a downstream task, two popular methods are full fine-tuning (updating all the model parameters) and linear probing (updating only the last linear layer -- the "head"). It is well known that fine-tuning leads to better accuracy in-distribution (ID). However, in this paper, we find that fine-tuning can achieve worse accuracy than linear probing out-of-distribution (OOD) when the pretrained features are good and the distribution shift is large. On 10 distribution shift datasets (Breeds-Living17, Breeds-Entity30, DomainNet, CIFAR $\to$ STL, CIFAR10.1, FMoW, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-Sketch), fine-tuning obtains on average 2% higher accuracy ID but 7% lower accuracy OOD than linear probing. We show theoretically that this tradeoff between ID and OOD accuracy arises even in a simple setting: fine-tuning overparameterized two-layer linear networks. We prove that the OOD error of fine-tuning is high when we initialize with a fixed or random head -- this is because while fine-tuning learns the head, the lower layers of the neural network change simultaneously and distort the pretrained features. Our analysis suggests that the easy two-step strategy of linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT), sometimes used as a fine-tuning heuristic, combines the benefits of both fine-tuning and linear probing. Empirically, LP-FT outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing on the above datasets (1% better ID, 10% better OOD than full fine-tuning).

papers.title: Preference Tuning For Toxicity Mitigation Generalizes Across Languages
papers.research_question: Does preference tuning (specifically Direct Preference Optimization) using only English data generalize to reduce toxicity in multilingual open-ended generations across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: English-only Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) training significantly reduces toxicity in multilingual LLM generations across 17 languages, and this cross-lingual generalization is explained by the dual multilinguality property of MLP layers.
papers.conclusion: Safety preference tuning with DPO for toxicity mitigation generalizes across languages in a zero-shot manner, and this generalization is mechanistically explained by the dual multilinguality of toxic neurons and can be predicted by bilingual sentence retrieval.
papers.key_findings:
DPO training with only English data significantly reduces the probability of generating toxic continuations and the expected maximum toxicity across 17 languages for multiple multilingual LLMs.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals the dual multilinguality of MLP layers: value vectors encode multilingual toxic concepts and key vectors activate on toxic prompts across languages, and DPO suppresses these activations.
Bilingual sentence retrieval accuracy strongly correlates with the cross-lingual transferability of DPO detoxification, serving as a predictor.
The effectiveness of cross-lingual detoxification varies by language, with languages more similar to English (e.g., Romance and Germanic languages) showing greater toxicity reduction.
There is a trade-off between toxicity reduction and fluency (perplexity) after DPO training, with higher learning rates leading to more toxicity reduction but worse perplexity.
papers.limitation:
Language coverage is limited to high- and mid-resource languages due to the limitation of the multilingual toxicity evaluator Perspective API.
The analysis does not cover culture-specific toxicity reduction.
Mechanistic interpretability experiments are primarily done on the mGPT-1.3B model.
The study focuses on the DPO algorithm and does not explore other preference tuning algorithms.
future_direction: Exploration of other preference tuning algorithms such as PPO, KTO, ORPO, and CPO for cross-lingual detoxification.
Analysis of culture-specific toxicity reduction.
Extending mechanistic interpretability experiments to other models beyond mGPT-1.3B.
papers.abstract: Detoxifying multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) has become crucial due to their increasing global use. In this work, we explore zero-shot cross-lingual generalization of preference tuning in detoxifying LLMs. Unlike previous studies that show limited cross-lingual generalization for other safety tasks, we demonstrate that Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) training with only English data can significantly reduce toxicity in multilingual open-ended generations. For example, the probability of mGPT-1.3B generating toxic continuations drops from 46.8% to 3.9% across 17 different languages after training. Our results also extend to other multilingual LLMs, such as BLOOM, Llama3, and Aya-23. Using mechanistic interpretability tools like causal intervention and activation analysis, we identified the dual multilinguality property of MLP layers in LLMs, which explains the cross-lingual generalization of DPO. Finally, we show that bilingual sentence retrieval can predict the cross-lingual transferability of DPO preference tuning.

papers.title: Representation Stability in a Minimal Continual Learning Agent
papers.research_question: How do internal representations evolve and stabilize in a minimal continual learning agent over time?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that stability-plasticity trade-offs can emerge in a minimal continual learning agent with persistent state, using representational similarity metrics, without explicit architectural mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that minimal continual learning agents exhibit stability-plasticity trade-offs through representational self-similarity, providing a baseline for understanding learning dynamics without task optimization.
papers.key_findings:
The agent transitions from an initial plastic regime to a stable representational regime under consistent input.
A semantic perturbation causes a bounded decrease in representational similarity, followed by recovery and re-stabilization.
Representational stability does not imply stagnation; the state can grow in dimensionality while maintaining directional alignment.
These dynamics emerge without explicit regularization, replay, or architectural complexity.
Learning can be observed as state evolution independent of task performance.
papers.limitation:
The agent employs a simple token-frequency representation.
The representation grows without bound, raising questions about long-term scalability, memory efficiency, and compression.
The agent does not interact with an environment or influence its inputs, precluding the study of feedback-driven or embodied learning.
Similarity metrics capture only coarse-grained structural alignment and do not reflect higher-order semantic organization.
future_direction: Incorporating structured representations, dimensionality reduction, information-theoretic measures, and dynamical systems analysis.
Studying learning under physical constraints, delayed feedback, and real-time operation in robotics and autonomous systems.
Exploring embodied representations, sensorimotor coupling, and co-adaptation from neuroscience and brain-machine interfaces.
papers.abstract: Continual learning systems are increasingly deployed in environments where retraining or reset is infeasible, yet many approaches emphasize task performance rather than the evolution of internal representations over time. In this work, we study a minimal continual learning agent designed to isolate representational dynamics from architectural complexity and optimization objectives. The agent maintains a persistent state vector across executions and incrementally updates it as new textual data is introduced. We quantify representational change using cosine similarity between successive normalized state vectors and define a stability metric over time intervals. Longitudinal experiments across eight executions reveal a transition from an initial plastic regime to a stable representational regime under consistent input. A deliberately introduced semantic perturbation produces a bounded decrease in similarity, followed by recovery and restabilization under subsequent coherent input. These results demonstrate that meaningful stability plasticity tradeoffs can emerge in a minimal, stateful learning system without explicit regularization, replay, or architectural complexity. The work establishes a transparent empirical baseline for studying representational accumulation and adaptation in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Safety-Utility Conflicts Are Not Global: Surgical Alignment via Head-Level Diagnosis
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the safety-utility trade-off in LLMs by leveraging the modular heterogeneity of Transformers to identify and selectively update low-conflict attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety-utility conflicts in LLMs are structurally localized in specific attention heads, and proposes CAST, a framework that uses head-level diagnosis to selectively update low-conflict heads, thereby improving the safety-utility trade-off.
papers.conclusion: Safety-utility conflicts are not uniformly distributed, and by using head-level diagnosis to guide sparse updates, CAST enables targeted safety alignment while preserving reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-utility conflicts are sparse and concentrated in specific attention heads, not globally distributed.
Updating high-conflict heads leads to significant utility degradation, while updating low-conflict heads preserves utility.
CAST achieves a better Pareto frontier in the safety-utility trade-off compared to global methods.
The pre-alignment conflict score strongly correlates with post-alignment utility cost (Pearson r up to 0.99).
CAST synergizes with geometric optimization methods like PCGrad to further improve the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
The diagnosis is limited to Query Projections (Wq) and does not cover MLPs, which contain most parameters and store factual knowledge.
The conflict map is static and pre-alignment, which may not account for conflict drift during extended fine-tuning.
The diagnosis relies on specific calibration sets and may not generalize to specialized domains like coding or creative writing.
future_direction: Extend the diagnosis to MLP layers.
Develop dynamic diagnosis to track conflict drift during training.
Improve domain transfer by using more representative calibration sets.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently presents a multi-objective optimization conflict, often accompanied by an unintended degradation of general capabilities. Existing mitigation strategies typically rely on global gradient geometry to resolve these conflicts, yet they overlook Modular Heterogeneity within Transformers, specifically that the functional sensitivity and degree of conflict vary substantially across different attention heads. Such global approaches impose uniform update rules across all parameters, often resulting in suboptimal trade-offs by indiscriminately updating utility sensitive heads that exhibit intense gradient conflicts. To address this limitation, we propose Conflict-Aware Sparse Tuning (CAST), a framework that integrates head-level diagnosis with sparse fine-tuning. CAST first constructs a pre-alignment conflict map by synthesizing Optimization Conflict and Functional Sensitivity, which then guides the selective update of parameters. Experiments reveal that alignment conflicts in LLMs are not uniformly distributed. We find that the drop in general capabilities mainly comes from updating a small group of ``high-conflict'' heads. By simply skipping these heads during training, we significantly reduce this loss without compromising safety, offering an interpretable and parameter-efficient approach to improving the safety-utility trade-off.

papers.title: Deeper Insights Without Updates: The Power of In-Context Learning Over Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning capture implicit patterns better than fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns in tasks, and the authors propose circuit shift theory to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning significantly outperforms fine-tuning in capturing implicit patterns within specific tasks and exhibits greater adaptability in problem-solving approaches, as evidenced by notable shifts in model circuits.
papers.key_findings:
ICL achieves higher accuracy than fine-tuning on implicit pattern detection tasks across models and tasks.
ICL is more robust to misleading data and out-of-distribution data compared to fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning plateaus quickly with more data, showing diminishing returns for implicit pattern detection.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods do not show significant improvement over full-parameter fine-tuning for implicit pattern detection.
ICL induces larger circuit shifts than fine-tuning, indicating a more significant change in the model's problem-solving approach.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is constrained by the specific nature of the implicit pattern detection tasks, limited to certain domains.
Circuit Shift analysis relies on activation patching and sensitivity analysis, which require further refinement and validation across different models and tasks.
Computational resources required for fine-tuning, especially with large models, may limit the feasibility of such experiments in broader settings.
A detailed cost-benefit analysis comparing ICL and fine-tuning in terms of computational efficiency and performance is needed.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning and in-context learning (ICL) are two prevalent methods in imbuing large language models with task-specific knowledge. It is commonly believed that fine-tuning can surpass ICL given sufficient training samples as it allows the model to adjust its internal parameters based on the data. However, this paper presents a counterintuitive finding: For tasks with implicit patterns, ICL captures these patterns significantly better than fine-tuning. We developed several datasets featuring implicit patterns, such as sequences determining answers through parity or identifying reducible terms in calculations. We then evaluated the models' understanding of these patterns under both fine-tuning and ICL across models ranging from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The results indicate that models employing ICL can quickly grasp deep patterns and significantly improve accuracy. In contrast, fine-tuning, despite utilizing thousands of times more training samples than ICL, achieved only limited improvements. We also proposed circuit shift theory from a mechanistic interpretability's view to explain why ICL wins.

papers.title: SafeMERGE: Preserving Safety Alignment in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models via Selective Layer-Wise Model Merging
papers.research_question: How can practitioners retain task utility while improving safety, without relying on custom algorithms, and while using standard open-source libraries?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SafeMERGE, a lightweight post-fine-tuning framework that selectively merges fine-tuned LoRA layers with safety-aligned layers based on cosine similarity, restoring safety without compromising task utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeMERGE is an effective method for restoring safety in fine-tuned LLMs without sacrificing performance, establishing selective layer-wise merging as a robust strategy.
papers.key_findings:
SafeMERGE consistently reduces harmfulness while maintaining or improving task utility across multiple models and tasks.
Selective layer-wise merging outperforms baselines like SafeLoRA, RESTA, and SafeInstruct in terms of safety-utility trade-off.
Cosine similarity is a more reliable metric than Euclidean distance for identifying unsafe layers.
The optimal cosine similarity threshold τ is stable across models and tasks, typically around 0.6-0.8.
Linear merging is sufficient and robust compared to other merging strategies like TIES.
papers.limitation:
Model and task selection is limited to four LLMs and two main tasks, with additional telecom tasks in appendix.
Safety evaluations rely on classifier-based assessment (Llama-Guard-3-8B) which has inherent limitations.
SafeMERGE requires an additional safe model fine-tuned on safety data.
The method is not evaluated against jailbreak-style adversarial attacks.
future_direction: Investigating domain-specific safety datasets for safe model training.
Deeper analysis of TIES merging behavior.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is a common practice to adapt generalist models to specialized domains. However, recent studies show that fine-tuning can erode safety alignment, causing LLMs to respond to harmful or unethical prompts. Many methods to realign safety have been proposed, but often introduce custom algorithms that are difficult to implement or compromise task utility. In this work, we propose SafeMERGE, a lightweight, post-fine-tuning framework that preserves safety while maintaining downstream performance. SafeMERGE selectively merges fine-tuned with safety-aligned model layers only when they deviate from safe behavior, measured by a cosine similarity criterion. Across three LLMs and two tasks, SafeMERGE consistently reduces harmful outputs compared to other defenses, with negligible or even positive impact on utility. Our results demonstrate that selective layer-wise merging offers an effective safeguard against the inadvertent loss of safety during fine-tuning, establishing SafeMERGE as a simple post-fine-tuning defense.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
papers.research_question: Under what circumstances do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) derive the most fine-grained latent features for safety—a low-frequency concept domain? How can we efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduce the cost of feature explanation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety-critical domains, which includes a pre-explanation evaluation metric to efficiently identify SAEs with strong safety domain-specific interpretability and reduces interpretation cost by 55% via segment-level simulation.
papers.conclusion: Safe-SAIL is a novel SAE interpretation framework that generates more granular safety feature explanations and reduces explanation costs by half, offering an internal perspective and methodology to address problems in LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Safe-SAIL reduces the cost of feature explanation by 55% through a segment-level simulation strategy while maintaining high correlation with token-level results.
The framework enables the identification of optimal SAE sparsity levels for safety domain-specific interpretability, which differs from the sparsity for minimal feature interference.
A comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is released, with human-readable explanations for 1,758 safety-related features across pornography, politics, violence, and terror domains.
Empirical analyses reveal how LLMs encode specific real-world risk entities (e.g., pornographic websites) and safety-critical concepts across model layers.
The work provides insights into model cognition and reasoning trajectories, particularly highlighting failure modes in low-resource languages where relevant safety features are not activated.
papers.limitation:
The safety feature database covers only four major risk domains; extending it to emerging safety concerns would broaden applicability.
Explanation quality depends on the explainer model's capabilities, which may vary across languages and technical domains.
Segment-level simulation offers efficiency gains but approximates token-level dynamics; applications requiring maximal granularity may benefit from hybrid approaches.
Evaluation metrics rely on empirically validated thresholds that could benefit from automated domain-adaptive tuning.
Analyses primarily identify strong correlational patterns; establishing causal mechanisms through controlled interventions remains an important next step.
future_direction: Extending the safety feature database to emerging safety concerns such as privacy leakage, model self-replication, or deceptive alignment.
Improving explanation quality across languages and technical domains.
Developing hybrid simulation approaches for applications requiring maximal granularity.
Automated domain-adaptive tuning for evaluation metrics.
Systematic causal validation of the broader feature set through controlled interventions.
papers.abstract: Increasing deployment of large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications raises significant safety concerns. Most existing safety research focuses on evaluating LLM outputs or specific safety tasks, limiting their ability to address broader, undefined risks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) facilitate interpretability research to clarify model behavior by explaining single-meaning atomic features decomposed from entangled signals. jHowever, prior applications on SAEs do not interpret features with fine-grained safety-related concepts, thus inadequately addressing safety-critical behaviors, such as generating toxic responses and violating safety regulations. For rigorous safety analysis, we must extract a rich and diverse set of safety-relevant features that effectively capture these high-risk behaviors, yet face two challenges: identifying SAEs with the greatest potential for generating safety concept-specific neurons, and the prohibitively high cost of detailed feature explanation. In this paper, we propose Safe-SAIL, a framework for interpreting SAE features within LLMs to advance mechanistic understanding in safety domains. Our approach systematically identifies SAE with best concept-specific interpretability, explains safety-related neurons, and introduces efficient strategies to scale up the interpretation process. We will release a comprehensive toolkit including SAE checkpoints and human-readable neuron explanations, which supports empirical analysis of safety risks to promote research on LLM safety.

papers.title: Uncovering Constraint-Based Behavior in Neural Models via Targeted\n Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does competition between linguistic constraints obscure underlying linguistic knowledge in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning re-weight constraints to uncover such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Models need to learn both linguistic constraints and their relative ranking; targeted fine-tuning can re-weight constraints to uncover dormant linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Mismatches between model and human linguistic behavior arise from either failure to learn constraints or failure to learn their ranking; targeted fine-tuning can help understand and adjust constraint rankings.
papers.key_findings:
English and Chinese models show an implicit causality (IC) bias, but Spanish and Italian models do not, due to competition with the pro-drop constraint.
Targeted fine-tuning demoting pro-drop in Spanish and Italian uncovers underlying IC knowledge.
Targeted fine-tuning promoting pro-drop in English and Chinese diminishes the IC bias.
Models learn linguistic constraints but may rank them incorrectly, leading to non-human-like behavior.
The failure to exhibit human-like behavior can be due to either not learning a constraint or not learning the correct constraint ranking.
future_direction: Pair behavioral analyses with representational probing to link model representations and behavior.
Explore constraint competition in different models like GPT-2.
Investigate other linguistic phenomena and constraints.
papers.abstract:
A growing body of literature has focused on detailing the linguistic
knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Existing work has
shown that non-linguistic biases in models can drive model behavior away from
linguistic generalizations. We hypothesized that competing linguistic processes
within a language, rather than just non-linguistic model biases, could obscure
underlying linguistic knowledge. We tested this claim by exploring a single
phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. While
human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, we find
cross-linguistic variation in model behavior. We show that competing processes
in a language act as constraints on model behavior and demonstrate that
targeted fine-tuning can re-weight the learned constraints, uncovering
otherwise dormant linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that
models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their
relative ranking, with mismatches in either producing non-human-like behavior.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
